The majority said: the one who drew near and descended is Jibril. It was also said it is the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning that his command and judgment drew near to him. The first is preferable.

It was said: according to those who say that the one who stood firm is Jibril and Muhammad, the meaning in their view is: then Muhammad drew near to his Lord with the nearness of honor, and then descended, that is, he fell in prostration. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾: that is, the measure between Jibril and Muhammad (ﷺ) was as much as two bow-lengths or less.

Or the measure between Muhammad and his Lord was two bow-lengths: that is, the measure of two Arabic bows.

Qab and qib, and qad and qid, all mean measure. Its meaning has been mentioned in al-Sihah (the lexicon).

al-Zajjaj said: that is, according to what you estimate; Allah, glorified is He, knows the measures of things, but He addresses us in the manner of address customary among us.

It was also said that "aw" here means waw (and): that is, "and nearer." It was also said it means bal (rather): that is, "rather nearer."

Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani and Abu Wail Shaqiq ibn Salamah said: ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ means two cubits in measure. The qaws is the cubit, by which everything is measured; this is the dialect of some Hijazis, and it was said it is the dialect of the Azd Shanuʾah.

al-Kisa'i said: "fa-kana qaba qawsayn" intends one bow.

﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾: that is, Jibril revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what he revealed, and in this is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him. Wahy is the casting of a thing swiftly, and from it is wahaa, which means haste. The pronoun in ʿabdihi (His servant) refers to Allah, as in His saying: ﴿He leaves not upon its back any creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. It was also said the meaning is: Allah revealed to His servant Jibril what He revealed. This was said by al-Rabiʿ, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah, and it was said that Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad.

It was said: Allah, glorified is He, has left vague what He revealed to Muhammad through Jibril, or what Allah revealed to His servant Jibril or to Muhammad, and did not explain it to us, so it is not for us to delve into its interpretation.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: what was revealed to him is ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] and ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Duha: 6], etc.

It was also said that Allah revealed to him: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and forbidden to the nations until your nation enters it."

It was also said that "ma" is for generality, not vagueness, and the intended meaning is everything that was revealed to him; but reading it as vagueness is preferable, because of the glorification it contains.

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: that is, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what his eye saw on the night of the Miʿraj. One says kadhdhabahu, when one says the lie to him and does not confirm him.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of the verse is that he saw something and was truthful about it.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿ma kadhaba﴾ with light emphasis; Hisham and Abu Jaʿfar read it with doubled emphasis. The "ma" in "ma raʾa" is relative or verbal in the accusative position as object of kadhaba, whether light or doubled.

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾

Al-Jumhur read ﴿afa-tumārūnahu﴾ with an alif, from al-mirāʾ (disputation), which is argument and contention. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta' and sukun on the mim, meaning: "will you then find it?" Abu ʿUbaydah preferred the second reading. He said: because they did not dispute with him but denied him. It is said: "marāhu ḥaqqahu," meaning he denied his right. And "maraytuhu ana": I denied him. He said: from it is the verse of the poet:

"If you satirize a man of truthfulness and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was not one to deny you."

That is, you denied him.

al-Mubarrad said: it is said "amraʾahu ʿan ḥaqqihi" or "ʿalā ḥaqqihi," when one prevents him from it and repels him.

It was said ʿalā here means ʿan.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi, Mujahid and al-Aʿraj read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta', from amraytu, meaning: "do you cause him to doubt and to be in doubt about him?"

Several exegetes said: the meaning according to the reading of the majority is "will you dispute with him by disputation," because they disputed with him when he was taken on the Night Journey; they said: "Describe for us the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis." That is, will you dispute with him with a disputation by which you seek to repel what he witnessed and knew?

The lam in His saying ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ is the one introducing the oath: that is, by Allah, he certainly saw him in another descent. The nazlah is one time of descending, so its accusative is either adverbial, or it is an accusative of the verbal noun standing in the place of a circumstantial clause: that is, he saw Jibril descending in another descent; or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun of emphasis: that is, he saw him with another seeing.

The majority of exegetes said: the meaning is that Muhammad saw Jibril another time. It was also said Muhammad saw his Lord another time with his heart.

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾: the adverbial phrase is accusative governed by ra'ahu (he saw). The sidr is the jujube tree (shajar al-nabq). This lote-tree is in the sixth heaven, as in the Sahih, and it was narrated that it is in the seventh heaven.

al-Muntaha: the place of ending, or it is a mimi verbal noun, and the intended meaning is the ending itself. It was said that to it the knowledge of all creatures ends, and none of them knows what lies beyond it. It was said that to it ascends what is lifted up from the earth. It was said that to it the souls of the martyrs ascend. And other things were said.

The attribution of the tree to al-Muntaha is an attribution of a thing to its place.

﴿عِنْدَها جَنَّةُ المَأْوى﴾ That is, beside that lote-tree (sidrah) is a garden known as the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa). It was called the Garden of Refuge because Adam took refuge in it. It is also said that the spirits of the believers take refuge in it.

The majority of reciters read jannatu with a nominative ending (ḍamma), making it the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding adverbial phrase (ẓarf).

ʿAlī, Abu l-Dardāʾ, Abu Hurayra, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, and Abu Sabra al-Juhanī read it as jannahu, a past-tense verb from janna yajunnu, meaning: the night's shelter covered him, or God's providing shelter for him concealed him.

Al-Akhfash said: it means "reached him," as you say: "the night covered him" (jannahu al-layl), meaning it concealed and overtook him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿إذْ يَغْشى السِّدْرَةَ ما يَغْشى﴾ The governing element of the adverbial phrase is "he saw" (ra'ahu) as well, and this is a time adverb, whereas the one before it was a place adverb. The verb ghashiya means to cover and conceal, and it also means to come to: one says "so-and-so comes to me (yaghshānī) every moment," meaning he comes to me. The vagueness in His words ﴿mā yaghshā﴾ conveys a grandeur that is not hidden. It is said that the lote-tree was covered by golden locusts, and it is said by bands of angels.

Mujāhid said: a green rafraf (silk canopy). It is also said a rafraf of green birds. It is also said that the command of God covered it. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation, to bring the wondrous image vividly before the mind, or to indicate continuous, renewing action.

﴿ما زاغَ البَصَرُ﴾ That is, the Prophet's ﷺ gaze did not turn away from what he saw. ﴿وما طَغى﴾ That is, it did not exceed what he saw. In this is a description of the Prophet's ﷺ courtesy (adab) in that station, for he did not look aside, his gaze did not wander, and he did not extend it to anything other than what he saw. It is also said: it did not exceed what he was commanded.

﴿لَقَدْ رَأى مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِ الكُبْرى﴾ That is, by God, on that night he saw of the great signs of his Lord what description cannot encompass. It is said he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. It is said he saw Gabriel in a green garment, filling the space between heaven and earth, with six hundred wings; so it is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere. Ḍaḥḥāk said: he saw the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. It is also said that it refers to everything he saw that night in his journey and his return. The "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), and the object of "ra'ā" is "al-kubrā." It is permissible that the object be omitted, meaning he saw a great thing of the signs of his Lord. It is also permissible that "min" be extra (zā'ida).

﴿أفَرَأيْتُمُ اللّاتَ والعُزّى ومَناةَ الثّالِثَةَ الأُخْرى﴾ When God, glory be to Him, related these accounts, He said to the polytheists, rebuking and reproaching them: "Have you considered?" That is, tell me about the deities you worship besides God: do they have any power that can be ascribed to them, and have they revealed anything to you as God revealed to Muḥammad, or are they lifeless objects that neither understand nor benefit?

Then He mentioned these three idols, which were famous among the Arabs and whose veneration was great.

Al-Wāḥidī and others said: they used to derive names for them from the names of God, the Exalted. From "Allāh" they formed "al-Lāt," from "al-ʿAzīz" they formed "al-ʿUzzā," which is the feminine of "al-aʿazz" in the sense of "the mighty one," and "Manāt," from "manā Allāh al-shay'" when He decreed it.

The majority read "al-Lāt" with a light tā', so it is said it is derived from the name of God, glory be to Him, as already mentioned. It is also said its root is "lāta yalītu," so the tā' is original. It is also said the tā' is extra and its root is "lawā yalwī," because they used to twist their necks toward it or wind around it and circumambulate it.

The reciters differed over whether it is stopped upon with a tā' or a hā'. The majority stopped upon it with a tā', while al-Kisā'ī stopped upon it with a hā'. Al-Zajjāj and al-Farrā' preferred stopping with a tā', following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, since it is written with a tā'.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujāhid, Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, Abu l-Jawzāʾ, Abu Ṣāliḥ, and Ḥumayd read "al-Lātt" with a doubled tā'. This reading is also transmitted from Ibn Kathīr. It is said it is the name of a man who used to knead sawiq (parched grain porridge) and feed it to the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave, worshipping him. So it is originally an active participle (ism fā'il) that became specific to this man. Mujāhid said: he was a man on the top of a mountain who made ḥays (a mixture of dates, butter and cheese) from its milk and butter and fed the pilgrims; he was in Baṭn Nakhla, and when he died they worshipped him.

Al-Kalbī said: he was a man from Thaqīf who had a flock of goats. It is said he was ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarab al-ʿAdwānī. This idol belonged to Thaqīf, and about it the poet says:

Do not support al-Lāt, for God will destroy it,
and how can one who cannot defend himself defend you?

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-Lāt is the name of an idol of Thaqīf, located in al-Ṭāʾif. Some Arabs stop upon it with a tā', and some with a hā'.

﴿والعُزّى﴾ is the idol of Quraysh and Banū Kināna.

Mujāhid said: it was a tree belonging to Ghaṭafān, which they worshipped. So the Prophet ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd, who cut it down. It is also said it was a she-devil who came to three acacia trees in Baṭn Nakhla.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: al-ʿUzzā is a white stone which they worshipped.

Qatāda said: it was a house in Baṭn Nakhla.

﴿ومَناةَ﴾ is the idol of Banū Hilāl. Ibn Hishām said: it is the idol of Hudhayl and Khuzāʿa.

Qatāda said: it belonged to the Anṣār.

The majority read "Manāt" with an alif without a hamza, while Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ḥumayd, Mujāhid and al-Sulamī read it with a long vowel and a hamza.

As for the majority's reading, its derivation is from manā yamnī, meaning to pour, because the blood of sacrificial animals was poured before it, by which they sought nearness to it.

As for the second reading, its derivation is from al-nawʾ, which is rain, because they used to seek rain before it through the rising of the stars (anwāʾ). It is also said that they are two dialects of the Arabs. Among what came in the first reading is the verse of Jarīr:

Do you threaten, O son of Taym, by Manāt?
Consider where your threat has led you.

Among what came in the second reading is the verse of al-Ḥārithī:

Has not Taym ibn ʿAbd Manāʾa reached,
regarding the secret between us, the son of Tamīm?

The majority of reciters stopped upon it with a tā' following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, while Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Muḥaysin stopped upon it with a hā'.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: Manāt is the name of an idol that was between Mecca and Medina. The hā' is for the feminine, and one may pause upon it with a tā', which is a dialect.

His words ﴿al-thālitha al-ukhrā﴾: this is a description of Manāt; He described her as "the third" and as "the other," and "the third" can only be "the other."

Abu l-Baqāʾ said: the description with "the other" is for emphasis. The description of the third as "the other" has been found problematic, since the Arabs only describe the second with it. Al-Khalīl said: He said that only to match the verse endings, as in His words: ﴿maʾārib ukhrā﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:18]. Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: there is inversion, and the intended sense is: "Have you considered al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, the other, and Manāt, the third?"

It is also said that describing her as "the other" is intended to magnify her, because she was great in the eyes of the polytheists. It is also said that it is for belittling and disparagement, and that what is meant is "the later and lowly one," as in His words: ﴿qālat ukhrāhum li-ūlāhum﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:38], meaning their followers said to their leaders.

Then God, glory be to Him, repeated His rebuke and reproach of them over a shameful saying they uttered, saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ That is, how can you ascribe to God what you dislike of females, while ascribing to yourselves what you love of males? It is said this refers to their saying that the angels are the daughters of God. It is also said the meaning is: how can you make al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, who are females by your own claim, partners with God? Their custom was to disdain females.

Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned that this naming and this division implied by the question is an unjust division, so He said: ﴿That, then, is an unfair division.﴾ The majority read ﴿ḍīzā﴾ with a quiescent yā' and without a hamza, while Ibn Kathīr read it with a quiescent hamza. The meaning: it is a division that departs from what is right, deviates from justice, and inclines away from truth.

Al-Akhfash said: it is said ḍāza fī al-ḥukm, meaning he was unjust; and ḍāzahu ḥaqqahu yaḍīzuhu ḍayzan, meaning he diminished and defrauded him of it. He said: it may be read with a hamza. He recited:

If you are absent from us, we shall diminish you, and if you are away, your right is diminished and your nose is humbled.

Al-Kisā'ī said: ḍāza yaḍīzu ḍayzan, and ḍāza yaḍūzu ḍawzan, when he transgressed, oppressed, defrauded and diminished. From it is the saying of the poet:

The Banū Asad were unjust in their judgment,
when they made the head like the tail.

Al-Farrā' said: some Arabs say ḍiʾzā with a hamza. Abu Ḥātim related from Abu Zayd that he heard the Arabs hamz ḍīzā. Al-Baghawī said: there is no fiʿlā with a kasra on the fā' in the adjectives of Arabic; it occurs only in nouns, like dhikrā. Al-Mu'arrij said: they disliked a ḍamma on the ḍād in ḍīzā and feared the change of the yā' into wāw, since it is from the wāw-root, so they gave the ḍād a kasra for this reason, as they said bīḍ as the plural of abyaḍ. Al-Zajjāj said likewise.

It is also said it is a verbal noun like dhikrā, so the meaning is: a division involving oppression and injustice.

Then God, glory be to Him, answered them with His words: ﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers﴾. That is, the idols, considered in terms of your claim that they are gods, are nothing but bare names, with nothing in them of the meaning of divinity you claim, for they neither see nor hear, neither understand nor comprehend, neither harm nor benefit. They are merely names you have given, you and your forefathers; the later ones imitated the earlier ones in this, and the sons followed the fathers.

In this is a belittling of their status that is not hidden, as one says in belittling a man: "He is nothing but a name" when he has no esteemed quality. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You worship besides Him only names you have named﴾ [Yūsuf 12:40]. One says: "I named him Zayd" and "I named him after Zayd." So His saying "sammaytumūhā" is a description of idols, and the pronoun refers to the names, not to the idols: that is, you made them names, not that you made names for them.

It is also said that His saying "they" (hiya) refers to the three names mentioned, but the first is preferable.

﴿mā anzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān﴾: that is, God has sent down no proof or evidence concerning them.

Muqātil said: He has not sent down to us or to you any book in which there is proof that they are gods, as you claim. Then He informed about them with His words: ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of naming and acting upon its consequences, they follow only conjecture, which does not avail them anything against the truth. He turned from address to the third person, turning away from them and belittling them, and said: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾, that is, what they incline toward and crave, without regard to what is the truth that must be followed.

The majority read "yattabiʿūna" with a yā' (third person). ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Ayyūb and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a tā' (second person). This reading is also transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭalḥa and Ibn Thābit.

﴿Indeed guidance has come to them from their Lord﴾: that is, the clear and evident explanation that they are not gods. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "yattabiʿūna." It is also permissible that it be a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ), but the first is preferable.

The meaning: how can they follow that when guidance from God has come to them, through the tongue of His Messenger whom God sent among them, made one of themselves.

﴿Or does man get whatever he wishes?﴾ The "am" here is the disjunctive one, implying "bal" and the interrogative hamza of denial. So He turned away from their following of conjecture, which is mere supposition, and from their following of the desires of souls and what they incline toward, and moved to deny that they should have what they wish, namely that the idols would benefit them and intercede for them.

Then He explained the denial that man should have what he wishes with His words: ﴿So to God belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾. That is, the affairs of the Hereafter and of this world, in their entirety, belong to God, mighty and majestic. So they have no affair with Him whatsoever. Among that is their vain wishes and their empty hopes.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 53, verses 1–26 (part 3 of 3):

Then He reinforced this and increased the refutation of what they desire, saying: ﴿How many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing﴾. "How many" (kam) here is the informative kam, which indicates multiplicity, and its position is nominative as a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), with the clause after it as its khabar (predicate). Because kam carries the sense of multiplicity, the pronoun in "their intercession" (shafa'atuhum) is plural while "angel" (malak) is singular. The meaning is a rebuke to them for what they wish for and hope for, namely the intercession of idols, when the angels, despite their great number of worshippers and their honour before Allah, intercede only for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for. How then about these inanimate objects that lack intellect and understanding? This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except after Allah gives permission﴾ for them to intercede for whomever He wills to be interceded for, ﴿and is pleased﴾ with the intercession for him because he is one of the people of monotheism (tawhid). The polytheists have no share in this, and Allah does not permit intercession for them nor is He pleased with it, because they are not among those deserving it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿By the star when it falls﴾ that he said: "When it descends."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him: "It is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) when it hangs down."

He also narrated from him: "Allah swore that Muhammad had neither gone astray nor erred."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also regarding His saying ﴿possessor of strength﴾, that he said: "Possessor of a fine form."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not see Jibril in his true form except twice. As for the first time, he asked him to show him his form, and he showed him his form, and it filled the horizon. As for the second time, he was with him when he ascended, and this is His saying: ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. He said: "The creation of Jibril."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), having six hundred wings." Ahmad also narrated it from him.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ that he said: "The rising place of the sun."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings."

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him regarding ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril, upon him two garments of green silk brocade (rafraf), which filled what lies between the heaven and the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ that he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ) who drew near and descended to his Lord."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "His Lord drew near and descended."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾ that he said: "Jibril drew near to him until he was the measure of one cubit or two cubits."

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The qab is the measure of a bow's length (qid), and the qawsayn are the two cubits (dhira'ayn)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he drew near (iqtaraba) to his Lord, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. Do you not see how close the bow is to its string?"

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ that he said: "His servant is Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Muslim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from him regarding ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ and ﴿And he saw him another time﴾ that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated similar from him.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw his Lord with his eye.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord twice: once with his sight and once with his heart."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) certainly saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic."

Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also that he said: "Do you wonder that friendship (khullah) is for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad?" Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Dharr that he said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'Light; how could I see Him?'"

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a light."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord with his heart and did not see Him with his eyes."

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah regarding His saying ﴿And he saw him another time﴾ that he said: "Jibril."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha)," and it is in the sixth heaven, where whatever ascends of the souls ends and is taken from it, and to it ends whatever descends from above it and is taken from it.
﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾. He said: "Moths of gold."

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Paradise is in the highest seventh heaven, and Hell is in the lowest seventh earth."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Al-Lat was a man who kneaded sawiq (a porridge of ground grain) for the pilgrims."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that al-'Uzza was in Batn Nakhlah, that al-Lat was at al-Ta'if, and that Manat was at Qudayd.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿unjust﴾ (diza) that he said: "Oppressive, having no right."

This surah is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah that it is Meccan except for one verse within it, namely His saying: ﴿Those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Najm was revealed in Mecca." He also narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was 'al-Najm'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and all the people prostrated with him, except a man whom I saw take a handful of dust and prostrate upon it. I later saw him killed as a disbeliever, and he was Umayyah ibn Khalaf."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The first surah with which the Prophet (ﷺ) openly recited was 'al-Najm'."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer, recited al-Najm, prostrated with us, and prolonged the prostration."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited al-Najm, and when he reached the prostration, he prostrated in it."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "I recited al-Najm in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate in it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to prostrate in 'al-Najm' in Mecca, but when he migrated to Medina he abandoned it."

He also narrated from him that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not prostrate in any part of al-Mufassal since he moved to Medina."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying ﴿By the star when it sets﴾: the definite article here is for the category (al-taʿrif li-l-jins, the generic definite), and the intended meaning is the class of stars. Several exegetes held this view, and from it is the verse of ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿah:

"The finest of stars in the sky is the Thurayya, and the Thurayya on earth is the adornment of women."

It was also said that the intended meaning is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). It is a name that became specific to it; the Arabs say "the star" and mean by it the Pleiades. This was said by Mujahid and others. al-Suddi said: the star here is Venus (al-Zuhara), because a people among the Arabs used to worship it. It was also said that "the star" here is the plant that has no stalk, as in His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6]. This was said by al-Akhfash.

It was also said that "the star" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said that "the star" is the Qur'an. It was called a star because it was revealed in installments, dispersed (munajjaman, mufarriqan), and the Arabs call dispersal tanjim, and the one who disperses munajjim. This was said by Mujahid, al-Farraʾ and others, and the first (view) is preferable.

al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of "the star" is the stars when they fall on the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the intended meaning is the stars by which devils are pelted. The meaning of its hawiy (falling) is its falling from a height. It is said: "the star hawa, yahwi, hawiyyan" when it falls from a height to a lower place. It was said that it means its setting, and it was said that it means its rising; the first is preferable, and this was said by al-Asmaʿi and others. From it is the verse of Zuhayr:

"Camels roam with it while it falls, like the falling of a bucket whose rope has released it."

It is also said: "hawa" in travel means to proceed. From it is the verse of the poet:

"While we were at al-Balakith, hastening, and the camels were rushing swiftly..."

"A thought passed over the heart of remembrance of you, weakly, so I could not proceed."

The meaning of falling, according to those who interpret "the star" as the Qur'an, is that it descended from above to below. As for those who say it is the tree without a stalk, or that it is Muhammad (ﷺ), then no correct meaning of falling appears. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is the implied verb of oath.

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: that is, Muhammad (ﷺ) did not stray from the truth and guidance, nor did he deviate from it. Ghayy is the opposite of rushd (right guidance), i.e., he did not become astray, nor did he speak falsehood. It was also said: he did not fail in what he sought. Ghayy also means failure, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"Whoever meets good, people will praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

In His saying "your companion" there is an indication that they are the ones who have knowledge of the reality of his condition. The address is to the Quraysh.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾: that is, his speech does not issue from desire, neither by the Qur'an nor by anything else. Here ʿan is in its proper sense.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: ʿan here means bi (with), that is, "by desire." Qatadah said: that is, he does not recite from his own desire.

﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾: that is, what he speaks is nothing but a revelation from Allah which He reveals to him.

His saying yuha (revealed) is an attribute of wahy (revelation), indicating continuous renewal, and indicating the negation of metaphor: that is, it is a true revelation, not merely a name.

﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾: al-quwa is the plural of quwwah (power). The meaning is that Jibril, whose powers are mighty, taught him. Most exegetes said this is what is meant, namely Jibril. al-Hasan said it is Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, but the first is preferable, and it is of the type of attributing an attribute to the one described.

﴿Possessor of strength; so he stood firm﴾: al-mirrah means strength and vigor in creation. It was also said: one of sound body and freedom from afflictions. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person, nor for one who is possessed of sound strength."

It was also said: one of firm understanding and solidity of judgment. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of everyone who has sound judgment and discerning intellect that he is dhu mirrah. From it is the verse of the poet:

"Before meeting you, I was one of firm strength; with me, for every disputant, is his balance."

Explaining mirrah by this is preferable, because strength and power were already conveyed by His saying "mighty in power." al-Jawhari said: mirrah is one of the four humors, and mirrah also means strength and intensity of intellect. The fa' in His saying fa-istawa is for conjunction with ʿallamahu, referring to Jibril: that is, he rose and returned to his place in the sky after he had taught Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

It was also said that the meaning of istawa is that he stood in the form in which Allah created him, because he used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of human beings. It was also said: the meaning is that the Qur'an stood firm in his chest (ﷺ).

al-Hasan said: "istawa" means Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, rose over the Throne.

﴿While he was on the highest horizon﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, Jibril stood firm while being on the highest horizon. By "the highest horizon" is meant the side of the east, which is above the side of the west. It was also said that the meaning is: he stood firm high up.

The ufuq is the region of the sky, and its plural is afaq.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the place from which the sun rises. It was also said: it refers to Jibril and the Prophet (ﷺ) on the highest horizon on the night of the Miʿraj. It is permissible that this clause be a new sentence.

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: that is, Jibril drew near after his standing firm on the highest horizon, that is, he approached the earth, and he descended and came down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with the revelation. It was said that there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: "then he descended and drew near." This was said by Ibn al-Anbari and others. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of dana and fa-tadalla is one: that is, he approached and increased in nearness, as you say "so-and-so drew near to me and came close," and if you say "he came close to me and drew near," it is permissible.

al-Farraʾ said: the fa' in fa-tadalla has the meaning of waw, and the sense is: "then Jibril descended and drew near." It is permissible, when the meanings of the two verbs are one, to place whichever you wish first.

The majority said: the one who drew near and descended is Jibril. It was also said it is the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning that his command and judgment drew near to him. The first is preferable.

It was said: according to those who say that the one who stood firm is Jibril and Muhammad, the meaning in their view is: then Muhammad drew near to his Lord with the nearness of honor, and then descended, that is, he fell in prostration. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾: that is, the measure between Jibril and Muhammad (ﷺ) was as much as two bow-lengths or less.

Or the measure between Muhammad and his Lord was two bow-lengths: that is, the measure of two Arabic bows.

Qab and qib, and qad and qid, all mean measure. Its meaning has been mentioned in al-Sihah (the lexicon).

al-Zajjaj said: that is, according to what you estimate; Allah, glorified is He, knows the measures of things, but He addresses us in the manner of address customary among us.

It was also said that "aw" here means waw (and): that is, "and nearer." It was also said it means bal (rather): that is, "rather nearer."

Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani and Abu Wail Shaqiq ibn Salamah said: ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ means two cubits in measure. The qaws is the cubit, by which everything is measured; this is the dialect of some Hijazis, and it was said it is the dialect of the Azd Shanuʾah.

al-Kisa'i said: "fa-kana qaba qawsayn" intends one bow.

﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾: that is, Jibril revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what he revealed, and in this is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him. Wahy is the casting of a thing swiftly, and from it is wahaa, which means haste. The pronoun in ʿabdihi (His servant) refers to Allah, as in His saying: ﴿He leaves not upon its back any creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. It was also said the meaning is: Allah revealed to His servant Jibril what He revealed. This was said by al-Rabiʿ, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah, and it was said that Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad.

It was said: Allah, glorified is He, has left vague what He revealed to Muhammad through Jibril, or what Allah revealed to His servant Jibril or to Muhammad, and did not explain it to us, so it is not for us to delve into its interpretation.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: what was revealed to him is ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] and ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Duha: 6], etc.

It was also said that Allah revealed to him: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and forbidden to the nations until your nation enters it."

It was also said that "ma" is for generality, not vagueness, and the intended meaning is everything that was revealed to him; but reading it as vagueness is preferable, because of the glorification it contains.

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: that is, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what his eye saw on the night of the Miʿraj. One says kadhdhabahu, when one says the lie to him and does not confirm him.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of the verse is that he saw something and was truthful about it.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿ma kadhaba﴾ with light emphasis; Hisham and Abu Jaʿfar read it with doubled emphasis. The "ma" in "ma raʾa" is relative or verbal in the accusative position as object of kadhaba, whether light or doubled.

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾

Al-Jumhur read ﴿afa-tumārūnahu﴾ with an alif, from al-mirāʾ (disputation), which is argument and contention. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta' and sukun on the mim, meaning: "will you then find it?" Abu ʿUbaydah preferred the second reading. He said: because they did not dispute with him but denied him. It is said: "marāhu ḥaqqahu," meaning he denied his right. And "maraytuhu ana": I denied him. He said: from it is the verse of the poet:

"If you satirize a man of truthfulness and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was not one to deny you."

That is, you denied him.

al-Mubarrad said: it is said "amraʾahu ʿan ḥaqqihi" or "ʿalā ḥaqqihi," when one prevents him from it and repels him.

It was said ʿalā here means ʿan.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi, Mujahid and al-Aʿraj read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta', from amraytu, meaning: "do you cause him to doubt and to be in doubt about him?"

Several exegetes said: the meaning according to the reading of the majority is "will you dispute with him by disputation," because they disputed with him when he was taken on the Night Journey; they said: "Describe for us the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis." That is, will you dispute with him with a disputation by which you seek to repel what he witnessed and knew?

The lam in His saying ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ is the one introducing the oath: that is, by Allah, he certainly saw him in another descent. The nazlah is one time of descending, so its accusative is either adverbial, or it is an accusative of the verbal noun standing in the place of a circumstantial clause: that is, he saw Jibril descending in another descent; or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun of emphasis: that is, he saw him with another seeing.

The majority of exegetes said: the meaning is that Muhammad saw Jibril another time. It was also said Muhammad saw his Lord another time with his heart.

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾: the adverbial phrase is accusative governed by ra'ahu (he saw). The sidr is the jujube tree (shajar al-nabq). This lote-tree is in the sixth heaven, as in the Sahih, and it was narrated that it is in the seventh heaven.

al-Muntaha: the place of ending, or it is a mimi verbal noun, and the intended meaning is the ending itself. It was said that to it the knowledge of all creatures ends, and none of them knows what lies beyond it. It was said that to it ascends what is lifted up from the earth. It was said that to it the souls of the martyrs ascend. And other things were said.

The attribution of the tree to al-Muntaha is an attribution of a thing to its place.

﴿عِنْدَها جَنَّةُ المَأْوى﴾ That is, beside that lote-tree (sidrah) is a garden known as the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa). It was called the Garden of Refuge because Adam took refuge in it. It is also said that the spirits of the believers take refuge in it.

The majority of reciters read jannatu with a nominative ending (ḍamma), making it the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding adverbial phrase (ẓarf).

ʿAlī, Abu l-Dardāʾ, Abu Hurayra, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, and Abu Sabra al-Juhanī read it as jannahu, a past-tense verb from janna yajunnu, meaning: the night's shelter covered him, or God's providing shelter for him concealed him.

Al-Akhfash said: it means "reached him," as you say: "the night covered him" (jannahu al-layl), meaning it concealed and overtook him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿إذْ يَغْشى السِّدْرَةَ ما يَغْشى﴾ The governing element of the adverbial phrase is "he saw" (ra'ahu) as well, and this is a time adverb, whereas the one before it was a place adverb. The verb ghashiya means to cover and conceal, and it also means to come to: one says "so-and-so comes to me (yaghshānī) every moment," meaning he comes to me. The vagueness in His words ﴿mā yaghshā﴾ conveys a grandeur that is not hidden. It is said that the lote-tree was covered by golden locusts, and it is said by bands of angels.

Mujāhid said: a green rafraf (silk canopy). It is also said a rafraf of green birds. It is also said that the command of God covered it. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation, to bring the wondrous image vividly before the mind, or to indicate continuous, renewing action.

﴿ما زاغَ البَصَرُ﴾ That is, the Prophet's ﷺ gaze did not turn away from what he saw. ﴿وما طَغى﴾ That is, it did not exceed what he saw. In this is a description of the Prophet's ﷺ courtesy (adab) in that station, for he did not look aside, his gaze did not wander, and he did not extend it to anything other than what he saw. It is also said: it did not exceed what he was commanded.

﴿لَقَدْ رَأى مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِ الكُبْرى﴾ That is, by God, on that night he saw of the great signs of his Lord what description cannot encompass. It is said he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. It is said he saw Gabriel in a green garment, filling the space between heaven and earth, with six hundred wings; so it is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere. Ḍaḥḥāk said: he saw the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. It is also said that it refers to everything he saw that night in his journey and his return. The "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), and the object of "ra'ā" is "al-kubrā." It is permissible that the object be omitted, meaning he saw a great thing of the signs of his Lord. It is also permissible that "min" be extra (zā'ida).

﴿أفَرَأيْتُمُ اللّاتَ والعُزّى ومَناةَ الثّالِثَةَ الأُخْرى﴾ When God, glory be to Him, related these accounts, He said to the polytheists, rebuking and reproaching them: "Have you considered?" That is, tell me about the deities you worship besides God: do they have any power that can be ascribed to them, and have they revealed anything to you as God revealed to Muḥammad, or are they lifeless objects that neither understand nor benefit?

Then He mentioned these three idols, which were famous among the Arabs and whose veneration was great.

Al-Wāḥidī and others said: they used to derive names for them from the names of God, the Exalted. From "Allāh" they formed "al-Lāt," from "al-ʿAzīz" they formed "al-ʿUzzā," which is the feminine of "al-aʿazz" in the sense of "the mighty one," and "Manāt," from "manā Allāh al-shay'" when He decreed it.

The majority read "al-Lāt" with a light tā', so it is said it is derived from the name of God, glory be to Him, as already mentioned. It is also said its root is "lāta yalītu," so the tā' is original. It is also said the tā' is extra and its root is "lawā yalwī," because they used to twist their necks toward it or wind around it and circumambulate it.

The reciters differed over whether it is stopped upon with a tā' or a hā'. The majority stopped upon it with a tā', while al-Kisā'ī stopped upon it with a hā'. Al-Zajjāj and al-Farrā' preferred stopping with a tā', following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, since it is written with a tā'.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujāhid, Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, Abu l-Jawzāʾ, Abu Ṣāliḥ, and Ḥumayd read "al-Lātt" with a doubled tā'. This reading is also transmitted from Ibn Kathīr. It is said it is the name of a man who used to knead sawiq (parched grain porridge) and feed it to the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave, worshipping him. So it is originally an active participle (ism fā'il) that became specific to this man. Mujāhid said: he was a man on the top of a mountain who made ḥays (a mixture of dates, butter and cheese) from its milk and butter and fed the pilgrims; he was in Baṭn Nakhla, and when he died they worshipped him.

Al-Kalbī said: he was a man from Thaqīf who had a flock of goats. It is said he was ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarab al-ʿAdwānī. This idol belonged to Thaqīf, and about it the poet says:

Do not support al-Lāt, for God will destroy it,
and how can one who cannot defend himself defend you?

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-Lāt is the name of an idol of Thaqīf, located in al-Ṭāʾif. Some Arabs stop upon it with a tā', and some with a hā'.

﴿والعُزّى﴾ is the idol of Quraysh and Banū Kināna.

Mujāhid said: it was a tree belonging to Ghaṭafān, which they worshipped. So the Prophet ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd, who cut it down. It is also said it was a she-devil who came to three acacia trees in Baṭn Nakhla.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: al-ʿUzzā is a white stone which they worshipped.

Qatāda said: it was a house in Baṭn Nakhla.

﴿ومَناةَ﴾ is the idol of Banū Hilāl. Ibn Hishām said: it is the idol of Hudhayl and Khuzāʿa.

Qatāda said: it belonged to the Anṣār.

The majority read "Manāt" with an alif without a hamza, while Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ḥumayd, Mujāhid and al-Sulamī read it with a long vowel and a hamza.

As for the majority's reading, its derivation is from manā yamnī, meaning to pour, because the blood of sacrificial animals was poured before it, by which they sought nearness to it.

As for the second reading, its derivation is from al-nawʾ, which is rain, because they used to seek rain before it through the rising of the stars (anwāʾ). It is also said that they are two dialects of the Arabs. Among what came in the first reading is the verse of Jarīr:

Do you threaten, O son of Taym, by Manāt?
Consider where your threat has led you.

Among what came in the second reading is the verse of al-Ḥārithī:

Has not Taym ibn ʿAbd Manāʾa reached,
regarding the secret between us, the son of Tamīm?

The majority of reciters stopped upon it with a tā' following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, while Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Muḥaysin stopped upon it with a hā'.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: Manāt is the name of an idol that was between Mecca and Medina. The hā' is for the feminine, and one may pause upon it with a tā', which is a dialect.

His words ﴿al-thālitha al-ukhrā﴾: this is a description of Manāt; He described her as "the third" and as "the other," and "the third" can only be "the other."

Abu l-Baqāʾ said: the description with "the other" is for emphasis. The description of the third as "the other" has been found problematic, since the Arabs only describe the second with it. Al-Khalīl said: He said that only to match the verse endings, as in His words: ﴿maʾārib ukhrā﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:18]. Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: there is inversion, and the intended sense is: "Have you considered al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, the other, and Manāt, the third?"

It is also said that describing her as "the other" is intended to magnify her, because she was great in the eyes of the polytheists. It is also said that it is for belittling and disparagement, and that what is meant is "the later and lowly one," as in His words: ﴿qālat ukhrāhum li-ūlāhum﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:38], meaning their followers said to their leaders.

Then God, glory be to Him, repeated His rebuke and reproach of them over a shameful saying they uttered, saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ That is, how can you ascribe to God what you dislike of females, while ascribing to yourselves what you love of males? It is said this refers to their saying that the angels are the daughters of God. It is also said the meaning is: how can you make al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, who are females by your own claim, partners with God? Their custom was to disdain females.

Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned that this naming and this division implied by the question is an unjust division, so He said: ﴿That, then, is an unfair division.﴾ The majority read ﴿ḍīzā﴾ with a quiescent yā' and without a hamza, while Ibn Kathīr read it with a quiescent hamza. The meaning: it is a division that departs from what is right, deviates from justice, and inclines away from truth.

Al-Akhfash said: it is said ḍāza fī al-ḥukm, meaning he was unjust; and ḍāzahu ḥaqqahu yaḍīzuhu ḍayzan, meaning he diminished and defrauded him of it. He said: it may be read with a hamza. He recited:

If you are absent from us, we shall diminish you, and if you are away, your right is diminished and your nose is humbled.

Al-Kisā'ī said: ḍāza yaḍīzu ḍayzan, and ḍāza yaḍūzu ḍawzan, when he transgressed, oppressed, defrauded and diminished. From it is the saying of the poet:

The Banū Asad were unjust in their judgment,
when they made the head like the tail.

Al-Farrā' said: some Arabs say ḍiʾzā with a hamza. Abu Ḥātim related from Abu Zayd that he heard the Arabs hamz ḍīzā. Al-Baghawī said: there is no fiʿlā with a kasra on the fā' in the adjectives of Arabic; it occurs only in nouns, like dhikrā. Al-Mu'arrij said: they disliked a ḍamma on the ḍād in ḍīzā and feared the change of the yā' into wāw, since it is from the wāw-root, so they gave the ḍād a kasra for this reason, as they said bīḍ as the plural of abyaḍ. Al-Zajjāj said likewise.

It is also said it is a verbal noun like dhikrā, so the meaning is: a division involving oppression and injustice.

Then God, glory be to Him, answered them with His words: ﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers﴾. That is, the idols, considered in terms of your claim that they are gods, are nothing but bare names, with nothing in them of the meaning of divinity you claim, for they neither see nor hear, neither understand nor comprehend, neither harm nor benefit. They are merely names you have given, you and your forefathers; the later ones imitated the earlier ones in this, and the sons followed the fathers.

In this is a belittling of their status that is not hidden, as one says in belittling a man: "He is nothing but a name" when he has no esteemed quality. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You worship besides Him only names you have named﴾ [Yūsuf 12:40]. One says: "I named him Zayd" and "I named him after Zayd." So His saying "sammaytumūhā" is a description of idols, and the pronoun refers to the names, not to the idols: that is, you made them names, not that you made names for them.

It is also said that His saying "they" (hiya) refers to the three names mentioned, but the first is preferable.

﴿mā anzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān﴾: that is, God has sent down no proof or evidence concerning them.

Muqātil said: He has not sent down to us or to you any book in which there is proof that they are gods, as you claim. Then He informed about them with His words: ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of naming and acting upon its consequences, they follow only conjecture, which does not avail them anything against the truth. He turned from address to the third person, turning away from them and belittling them, and said: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾, that is, what they incline toward and crave, without regard to what is the truth that must be followed.

The majority read "yattabiʿūna" with a yā' (third person). ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Ayyūb and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a tā' (second person). This reading is also transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭalḥa and Ibn Thābit.

﴿Indeed guidance has come to them from their Lord﴾: that is, the clear and evident explanation that they are not gods. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "yattabiʿūna." It is also permissible that it be a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ), but the first is preferable.

The meaning: how can they follow that when guidance from God has come to them, through the tongue of His Messenger whom God sent among them, made one of themselves.

﴿Or does man get whatever he wishes?﴾ The "am" here is the disjunctive one, implying "bal" and the interrogative hamza of denial. So He turned away from their following of conjecture, which is mere supposition, and from their following of the desires of souls and what they incline toward, and moved to deny that they should have what they wish, namely that the idols would benefit them and intercede for them.

Then He explained the denial that man should have what he wishes with His words: ﴿So to God belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾. That is, the affairs of the Hereafter and of this world, in their entirety, belong to God, mighty and majestic. So they have no affair with Him whatsoever. Among that is their vain wishes and their empty hopes.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 53, verses 1–26 (part 3 of 3):

Then He reinforced this and increased the refutation of what they desire, saying: ﴿How many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing﴾. "How many" (kam) here is the informative kam, which indicates multiplicity, and its position is nominative as a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), with the clause after it as its khabar (predicate). Because kam carries the sense of multiplicity, the pronoun in "their intercession" (shafa'atuhum) is plural while "angel" (malak) is singular. The meaning is a rebuke to them for what they wish for and hope for, namely the intercession of idols, when the angels, despite their great number of worshippers and their honour before Allah, intercede only for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for. How then about these inanimate objects that lack intellect and understanding? This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except after Allah gives permission﴾ for them to intercede for whomever He wills to be interceded for, ﴿and is pleased﴾ with the intercession for him because he is one of the people of monotheism (tawhid). The polytheists have no share in this, and Allah does not permit intercession for them nor is He pleased with it, because they are not among those deserving it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿By the star when it falls﴾ that he said: "When it descends."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him: "It is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) when it hangs down."

He also narrated from him: "Allah swore that Muhammad had neither gone astray nor erred."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also regarding His saying ﴿possessor of strength﴾, that he said: "Possessor of a fine form."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not see Jibril in his true form except twice. As for the first time, he asked him to show him his form, and he showed him his form, and it filled the horizon. As for the second time, he was with him when he ascended, and this is His saying: ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. He said: "The creation of Jibril."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), having six hundred wings." Ahmad also narrated it from him.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ that he said: "The rising place of the sun."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings."

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him regarding ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril, upon him two garments of green silk brocade (rafraf), which filled what lies between the heaven and the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ that he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ) who drew near and descended to his Lord."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "His Lord drew near and descended."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾ that he said: "Jibril drew near to him until he was the measure of one cubit or two cubits."

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The qab is the measure of a bow's length (qid), and the qawsayn are the two cubits (dhira'ayn)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he drew near (iqtaraba) to his Lord, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. Do you not see how close the bow is to its string?"

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ that he said: "His servant is Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Muslim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from him regarding ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ and ﴿And he saw him another time﴾ that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated similar from him.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw his Lord with his eye.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord twice: once with his sight and once with his heart."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) certainly saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic."

Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also that he said: "Do you wonder that friendship (khullah) is for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad?" Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Dharr that he said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'Light; how could I see Him?'"

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a light."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord with his heart and did not see Him with his eyes."

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah regarding His saying ﴿And he saw him another time﴾ that he said: "Jibril."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha)," and it is in the sixth heaven, where whatever ascends of the souls ends and is taken from it, and to it ends whatever descends from above it and is taken from it.
﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾. He said: "Moths of gold."

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Paradise is in the highest seventh heaven, and Hell is in the lowest seventh earth."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Al-Lat was a man who kneaded sawiq (a porridge of ground grain) for the pilgrims."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that al-'Uzza was in Batn Nakhlah, that al-Lat was at al-Ta'if, and that Manat was at Qudayd.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿unjust﴾ (diza) that he said: "Oppressive, having no right."

This surah is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah that it is Meccan except for one verse within it, namely His saying: ﴿Those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Najm was revealed in Mecca." He also narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was 'al-Najm'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and all the people prostrated with him, except a man whom I saw take a handful of dust and prostrate upon it. I later saw him killed as a disbeliever, and he was Umayyah ibn Khalaf."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The first surah with which the Prophet (ﷺ) openly recited was 'al-Najm'."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer, recited al-Najm, prostrated with us, and prolonged the prostration."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited al-Najm, and when he reached the prostration, he prostrated in it."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "I recited al-Najm in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate in it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to prostrate in 'al-Najm' in Mecca, but when he migrated to Medina he abandoned it."

He also narrated from him that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not prostrate in any part of al-Mufassal since he moved to Medina."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying ﴿By the star when it sets﴾: the definite article here is for the category (al-taʿrif li-l-jins, the generic definite), and the intended meaning is the class of stars. Several exegetes held this view, and from it is the verse of ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿah:

"The finest of stars in the sky is the Thurayya, and the Thurayya on earth is the adornment of women."

It was also said that the intended meaning is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). It is a name that became specific to it; the Arabs say "the star" and mean by it the Pleiades. This was said by Mujahid and others. al-Suddi said: the star here is Venus (al-Zuhara), because a people among the Arabs used to worship it. It was also said that "the star" here is the plant that has no stalk, as in His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6]. This was said by al-Akhfash.

It was also said that "the star" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said that "the star" is the Qur'an. It was called a star because it was revealed in installments, dispersed (munajjaman, mufarriqan), and the Arabs call dispersal tanjim, and the one who disperses munajjim. This was said by Mujahid, al-Farraʾ and others, and the first (view) is preferable.

al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of "the star" is the stars when they fall on the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the intended meaning is the stars by which devils are pelted. The meaning of its hawiy (falling) is its falling from a height. It is said: "the star hawa, yahwi, hawiyyan" when it falls from a height to a lower place. It was said that it means its setting, and it was said that it means its rising; the first is preferable, and this was said by al-Asmaʿi and others. From it is the verse of Zuhayr:

"Camels roam with it while it falls, like the falling of a bucket whose rope has released it."

It is also said: "hawa" in travel means to proceed. From it is the verse of the poet:

"While we were at al-Balakith, hastening, and the camels were rushing swiftly..."

"A thought passed over the heart of remembrance of you, weakly, so I could not proceed."

The meaning of falling, according to those who interpret "the star" as the Qur'an, is that it descended from above to below. As for those who say it is the tree without a stalk, or that it is Muhammad (ﷺ), then no correct meaning of falling appears. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is the implied verb of oath.

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: that is, Muhammad (ﷺ) did not stray from the truth and guidance, nor did he deviate from it. Ghayy is the opposite of rushd (right guidance), i.e., he did not become astray, nor did he speak falsehood. It was also said: he did not fail in what he sought. Ghayy also means failure, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"Whoever meets good, people will praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

In His saying "your companion" there is an indication that they are the ones who have knowledge of the reality of his condition. The address is to the Quraysh.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾: that is, his speech does not issue from desire, neither by the Qur'an nor by anything else. Here ʿan is in its proper sense.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: ʿan here means bi (with), that is, "by desire." Qatadah said: that is, he does not recite from his own desire.

﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾: that is, what he speaks is nothing but a revelation from Allah which He reveals to him.

His saying yuha (revealed) is an attribute of wahy (revelation), indicating continuous renewal, and indicating the negation of metaphor: that is, it is a true revelation, not merely a name.

﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾: al-quwa is the plural of quwwah (power). The meaning is that Jibril, whose powers are mighty, taught him. Most exegetes said this is what is meant, namely Jibril. al-Hasan said it is Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, but the first is preferable, and it is of the type of attributing an attribute to the one described.

﴿Possessor of strength; so he stood firm﴾: al-mirrah means strength and vigor in creation. It was also said: one of sound body and freedom from afflictions. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person, nor for one who is possessed of sound strength."

It was also said: one of firm understanding and solidity of judgment. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of everyone who has sound judgment and discerning intellect that he is dhu mirrah. From it is the verse of the poet:

"Before meeting you, I was one of firm strength; with me, for every disputant, is his balance."

Explaining mirrah by this is preferable, because strength and power were already conveyed by His saying "mighty in power." al-Jawhari said: mirrah is one of the four humors, and mirrah also means strength and intensity of intellect. The fa' in His saying fa-istawa is for conjunction with ʿallamahu, referring to Jibril: that is, he rose and returned to his place in the sky after he had taught Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

It was also said that the meaning of istawa is that he stood in the form in which Allah created him, because he used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of human beings. It was also said: the meaning is that the Qur'an stood firm in his chest (ﷺ).

al-Hasan said: "istawa" means Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, rose over the Throne.

﴿While he was on the highest horizon﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, Jibril stood firm while being on the highest horizon. By "the highest horizon" is meant the side of the east, which is above the side of the west. It was also said that the meaning is: he stood firm high up.

The ufuq is the region of the sky, and its plural is afaq.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the place from which the sun rises. It was also said: it refers to Jibril and the Prophet (ﷺ) on the highest horizon on the night of the Miʿraj. It is permissible that this clause be a new sentence.

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: that is, Jibril drew near after his standing firm on the highest horizon, that is, he approached the earth, and he descended and came down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with the revelation. It was said that there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: "then he descended and drew near." This was said by Ibn al-Anbari and others. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of dana and fa-tadalla is one: that is, he approached and increased in nearness, as you say "so-and-so drew near to me and came close," and if you say "he came close to me and drew near," it is permissible.

al-Farraʾ said: the fa' in fa-tadalla has the meaning of waw, and the sense is: "then Jibril descended and drew near." It is permissible, when the meanings of the two verbs are one, to place whichever you wish first.

The majority said: the one who drew near and descended is Jibril. It was also said it is the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning that his command and judgment drew near to him. The first is preferable.

It was said: according to those who say that the one who stood firm is Jibril and Muhammad, the meaning in their view is: then Muhammad drew near to his Lord with the nearness of honor, and then descended, that is, he fell in prostration. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾: that is, the measure between Jibril and Muhammad (ﷺ) was as much as two bow-lengths or less.

Or the measure between Muhammad and his Lord was two bow-lengths: that is, the measure of two Arabic bows.

Qab and qib, and qad and qid, all mean measure. Its meaning has been mentioned in al-Sihah (the lexicon).

al-Zajjaj said: that is, according to what you estimate; Allah, glorified is He, knows the measures of things, but He addresses us in the manner of address customary among us.

It was also said that "aw" here means waw (and): that is, "and nearer." It was also said it means bal (rather): that is, "rather nearer."

Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani and Abu Wail Shaqiq ibn Salamah said: ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ means two cubits in measure. The qaws is the cubit, by which everything is measured; this is the dialect of some Hijazis, and it was said it is the dialect of the Azd Shanuʾah.

al-Kisa'i said: "fa-kana qaba qawsayn" intends one bow.

﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾: that is, Jibril revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what he revealed, and in this is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him. Wahy is the casting of a thing swiftly, and from it is wahaa, which means haste. The pronoun in ʿabdihi (His servant) refers to Allah, as in His saying: ﴿He leaves not upon its back any creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. It was also said the meaning is: Allah revealed to His servant Jibril what He revealed. This was said by al-Rabiʿ, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah, and it was said that Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad.

It was said: Allah, glorified is He, has left vague what He revealed to Muhammad through Jibril, or what Allah revealed to His servant Jibril or to Muhammad, and did not explain it to us, so it is not for us to delve into its interpretation.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: what was revealed to him is ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] and ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Duha: 6], etc.

It was also said that Allah revealed to him: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and forbidden to the nations until your nation enters it."

It was also said that "ma" is for generality, not vagueness, and the intended meaning is everything that was revealed to him; but reading it as vagueness is preferable, because of the glorification it contains.

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: that is, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what his eye saw on the night of the Miʿraj. One says kadhdhabahu, when one says the lie to him and does not confirm him.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of the verse is that he saw something and was truthful about it.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿ma kadhaba﴾ with light emphasis; Hisham and Abu Jaʿfar read it with doubled emphasis. The "ma" in "ma raʾa" is relative or verbal in the accusative position as object of kadhaba, whether light or doubled.

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾

Al-Jumhur read ﴿afa-tumārūnahu﴾ with an alif, from al-mirāʾ (disputation), which is argument and contention. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta' and sukun on the mim, meaning: "will you then find it?" Abu ʿUbaydah preferred the second reading. He said: because they did not dispute with him but denied him. It is said: "marāhu ḥaqqahu," meaning he denied his right. And "maraytuhu ana": I denied him. He said: from it is the verse of the poet:

"If you satirize a man of truthfulness and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was not one to deny you."

That is, you denied him.

al-Mubarrad said: it is said "amraʾahu ʿan ḥaqqihi" or "ʿalā ḥaqqihi," when one prevents him from it and repels him.

It was said ʿalā here means ʿan.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi, Mujahid and al-Aʿraj read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta', from amraytu, meaning: "do you cause him to doubt and to be in doubt about him?"

Several exegetes said: the meaning according to the reading of the majority is "will you dispute with him by disputation," because they disputed with him when he was taken on the Night Journey; they said: "Describe for us the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis." That is, will you dispute with him with a disputation by which you seek to repel what he witnessed and knew?

The lam in His saying ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ is the one introducing the oath: that is, by Allah, he certainly saw him in another descent. The nazlah is one time of descending, so its accusative is either adverbial, or it is an accusative of the verbal noun standing in the place of a circumstantial clause: that is, he saw Jibril descending in another descent; or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun of emphasis: that is, he saw him with another seeing.

The majority of exegetes said: the meaning is that Muhammad saw Jibril another time. It was also said Muhammad saw his Lord another time with his heart.

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾: the adverbial phrase is accusative governed by ra'ahu (he saw). The sidr is the jujube tree (shajar al-nabq). This lote-tree is in the sixth heaven, as in the Sahih, and it was narrated that it is in the seventh heaven.

al-Muntaha: the place of ending, or it is a mimi verbal noun, and the intended meaning is the ending itself. It was said that to it the knowledge of all creatures ends, and none of them knows what lies beyond it. It was said that to it ascends what is lifted up from the earth. It was said that to it the souls of the martyrs ascend. And other things were said.

The attribution of the tree to al-Muntaha is an attribution of a thing to its place.

﴿عِنْدَها جَنَّةُ المَأْوى﴾ That is, beside that lote-tree (sidrah) is a garden known as the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa). It was called the Garden of Refuge because Adam took refuge in it. It is also said that the spirits of the believers take refuge in it.

The majority of reciters read jannatu with a nominative ending (ḍamma), making it the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding adverbial phrase (ẓarf).

ʿAlī, Abu l-Dardāʾ, Abu Hurayra, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, and Abu Sabra al-Juhanī read it as jannahu, a past-tense verb from janna yajunnu, meaning: the night's shelter covered him, or God's providing shelter for him concealed him.

Al-Akhfash said: it means "reached him," as you say: "the night covered him" (jannahu al-layl), meaning it concealed and overtook him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿إذْ يَغْشى السِّدْرَةَ ما يَغْشى﴾ The governing element of the adverbial phrase is "he saw" (ra'ahu) as well, and this is a time adverb, whereas the one before it was a place adverb. The verb ghashiya means to cover and conceal, and it also means to come to: one says "so-and-so comes to me (yaghshānī) every moment," meaning he comes to me. The vagueness in His words ﴿mā yaghshā﴾ conveys a grandeur that is not hidden. It is said that the lote-tree was covered by golden locusts, and it is said by bands of angels.

Mujāhid said: a green rafraf (silk canopy). It is also said a rafraf of green birds. It is also said that the command of God covered it. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation, to bring the wondrous image vividly before the mind, or to indicate continuous, renewing action.

﴿ما زاغَ البَصَرُ﴾ That is, the Prophet's ﷺ gaze did not turn away from what he saw. ﴿وما طَغى﴾ That is, it did not exceed what he saw. In this is a description of the Prophet's ﷺ courtesy (adab) in that station, for he did not look aside, his gaze did not wander, and he did not extend it to anything other than what he saw. It is also said: it did not exceed what he was commanded.

﴿لَقَدْ رَأى مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِ الكُبْرى﴾ That is, by God, on that night he saw of the great signs of his Lord what description cannot encompass. It is said he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. It is said he saw Gabriel in a green garment, filling the space between heaven and earth, with six hundred wings; so it is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere. Ḍaḥḥāk said: he saw the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. It is also said that it refers to everything he saw that night in his journey and his return.
