"A phantom from Qutaylah passed by after her cord had been severed from our cord and cut off."

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "alamma al-rajul" means he committed minor sins, and it is said it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Another recited:

"With Zaynab, approach me before the caravan departs, and say: if you have grown weary of us, the heart has not grown weary of you."

The scholars differed in interpreting this lamam mentioned in the verse. The majority hold that it means minor sins. It has been said it is what falls short of fornication, such as a kiss, a glance, or a look. It has been said it is the man who approaches a sin and then repents. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and others said this, and from it is the saying:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much; and what servant of Yours is there who has not approached sin?"

Al-Zajjāj preferred this view, as did al-Naḥḥās. It has been said it is the sins of the Jāhiliyyah, for Allah does not hold one accountable for them in Islam. Niftawayh said: it is that a person commits a sin he was not accustomed to. He said: the Arabs say, "you do not visit us except occasionally," that is, from time to time. He said: it is not that one approaches and does not act, because the Arabs do not say "he approached us" except when he has acted, not when he intended and did not act. The more preferred is the first view.

His words ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ are a justification for what the exception contains: that is, even if that [minor sin] is outside the ruling of being held accountable, it is nonetheless a sin that requires the forgiveness of Allah and needs His mercy. It has been said that He, glory be to Him, forgives whoever repents from his sin.

Then He mentioned His comprehensive knowledge of the states of His servants, saying: ﴿He knows you best when He produced you from the earth.﴾ That is: He created you from it within the creation of your father Ādam. It has been said that the intended is Ādam, for He created him from clay. ﴿And when you were embryos﴾ That is: He knows best your state at the time you were embryos. The word ajinnah is the plural of janīn, which is the child as long as it is in the womb; it was so named because of its being concealed (ijtinān), that is, its being hidden. For this reason He said ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾. So one who has come out of the womb is not called a janīn. The sentence is independent, establishing what precedes it. ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ That is: do not praise yourselves, do not declare yourselves free of sins, and do not commend yourselves. For abandoning the self-justification of the soul is further from ostentation (riyāʾ) and closer to humility (khushūʿ). The sentence ﴿He knows best who has been righteous﴾ is independent, confirming the prohibition: that is, He knows best who has been mindful of Allah's punishment and sincerely directed his deed to Him.

Al-Ḥasan said: Allah, glory be to Him, knows of every soul what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, had explained the ignorance of the polytheists in general, He singled out some of them for censure, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is: who turned away from good and turned aside from following the truth.

﴿And gave little and then held back.﴾ That is: he gave a small gift, or gave something little, then cut that off and withheld from it. The origin of akdā is from kudyah, which is hardness. It is said of one who dug a well and then reached a rock in which digging was impossible for him: "he has akdā." Then the Arabs used it for one who gave but did not complete, and for one who sought something but did not reach its end. From it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"He gave little, then his giving was cut off; and whoever spends kindness among people is praised."

Al-Kisāʾī and Abū Zayd said: it is said "his fingers were hardened" when they were worn out from digging; and "his hand became hard" when it was tired and did not accomplish anything; and "the land became hard" when its vegetation became scant; and "I made the man hold back from the thing" when I turned him away from it; and "the man held back" when his goodness became scant.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of the verse is: he withheld from the gift and cut it off.

Al-Mubarrad said: he refused with a severe refusal.

Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, but some of the polytheists reproached him, so he abandoned it and returned to his polytheism.

Muqātil said: al-Walīd had praised the Qur'an, then withheld from it, so he gave a little of his tongue's goodness and then cut it off.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: it was revealed concerning Abū Jahl.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning is: does this one who withheld have knowledge of what is hidden from him of the matter of punishment, so that he knows it?

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā﴾ ﴿and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ That is: has he not been told and has he not been given news of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā, meaning his books, which are the Torah; and of what is in the scriptures of Ibrāhīm who fulfilled: that is, who completed and perfected what he was commanded.

The exegetes said: that is, he conveyed to his people what he was commanded and delivered it to them. It has been said: he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he had covenanted with Allah.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained what is in their two scriptures, saying: ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.﴾ That is: no soul bearing a burden will carry the burden of another soul. Its meaning is: no soul will be seized for the sin of another. Here "that" (an) is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence following it. The position of the sentence is in the genitive as an appositive (badal) of "the scriptures of Mūsā and the scriptures of Ibrāhīm," or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The tafsīr of this verse has already passed in the surah of al-Anʿām.

**Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani, commentary on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. It is coordinated with His saying ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this too is among what is in the scrolls of Musa (Moses). The meaning is: he has no reward except the recompense of his effort and the requital of his deeds, and no one's deed benefits anyone else. This general statement is specified (*makhsus*) by such verses as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur: 21], and by what is reported concerning the intercession of the prophets and angels for the servants, the legitimacy of the living supplicating for the dead, and similar matters. Whoever said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) by such matters has not been correct, for a specific text does not abrogate a general one; rather, it specifies it. Thus, every proof that establishes that a person benefits from something that is not of his own striving is a specifier for the generality contained in this verse.

﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾: that is, it will be presented to him and disclosed to him on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then he will be recompensed for it﴾: that is, a person will be recompensed for his effort. One says, "Allah recompensed him for his deed" and "recompensed him for his deed" (using different prepositions).

The pronoun in the nominative (the subject of the verb) refers to the man, and the pronoun in the accusative (the object) refers to his effort.

It has been said that the accusative pronoun refers to the recompense mentioned later, which is His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾. In that case the pronoun refers to something mentioned after it, which explains it. It is also permissible for the accusative pronoun to refer to the recompense (*al-jaza'*), which is the verbal noun of *yujziyahu*, and for ﴿the fullest recompense﴾ to be an explanation of the recompense implied by the verb, as in His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. Al-Akhfash said: "One says *jazaytuhu al-jaza'* and *jazaytuhu bil-jaza'*, and there is no difference between them."

﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾: that is, the return and the destination are to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else, so He will requite them for their deeds.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾, that he said: "The major sins are those for which Allah has named the Fire as a punishment, and the immoralities are those for which there is a prescribed legal penalty (*hadd*) in this world."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more resembling *al-lamam* (minor lapses) than what Abu Hurayrah reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eye is the look, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private part confirms this or denies it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The adultery of the two eyes is looking, the adultery of the two lips is kissing, the adultery of the two hands is grasping, and the adultery of the two feet is walking. The private part confirms this or denies it. If he has gone as far as his private part, he is an adulterer; otherwise, it is *al-lamam*."

Musaddad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah that he was asked about His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, and he said: "They are the glance, the squeeze, the kiss and the touching. When the circumcised part touches the circumcised part, the ritual bath becomes obligatory, and that is adultery."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it authentic, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It is the man who commits an immorality and then repents from it."

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
But which of Your servants has not committed lapses?"*

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It means except what has already passed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The *lamma* (lapse) of adultery is when one commits it, then repents and does not return to it; and the *lamma* of drinking wine is when one drinks it, then repents and does not return to it. That is *al-ilmam* (the occasional lapse)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*Al-lamam* is everything between the two limits: the limit of this world and the limit of the Hereafter. It is expiated by the prayer, and it is less than every offence that carries a legal consequence. As for the limit of this world, it is every prescribed penalty that Allah has ordained in this world. As for the limit of the Hereafter, it is everything that Allah has concluded with the Fire, deferring its punishment until the Hereafter."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* reported from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, when a young child of theirs died, would say, 'He is a *siddiq* (a truthful one).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'The Jews have lied. There is no soul that Allah creates in its mother's womb except that it is either wretched or blessed.' Then Allah revealed at that point ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾, the whole verse."

Ahmad, Muslim and Abu Dawud reported "from Zaynab bint Abi Salamah, that she was named Barrah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not praise yourselves; Allah knows best who is truly righteous among you. Name her Zaynab.'" (p-1424)

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and gave little and held back﴾, that he said: "He cut off. It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "He obeyed a little, then stopped."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab* and al-Daylami reported, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Do you know what His saying ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ means?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He fulfilled his day's work with four rak'ahs which he prayed, and he claimed that they were the prayer of *al-Duha* (the forenoon)." In its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is weak.

al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The shares of Islam are thirty shares, which no one completed before Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Allah said: ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾."

Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning the verse, that he said: "It means Ibrahim, who completed obedience in what he did with his son when he saw the vision. And what is in the scrolls of Musa is ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas, from his father, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled? He used to say every morning and evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17], to the end of the verse." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When *al-Najm* was revealed, and it reached ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾, he said: 'He fulfilled ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to His saying ﴿of the warnings of old﴾.'"

Abu Dawud, al-Nahhas (both in *al-Nasikh*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. Then Allah revealed after that ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. So Allah admitted the children into Paradise because of the righteousness of their fathers."

Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾, ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾, ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾, would say *istirja'* (*inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un*) and would humble himself."

al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad* and al-Baghawi in his *Tafsir* reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, that he said: "There is no reflecting on the Lord (*la fikrah fi al-Rabb*)."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 1 of 2):**

His words: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ That is, these people who do not believe in resurrection and what follows it of the Abode of the Hereafter, namely the disbelievers, add to their disbelief an abominable saying and an ignorant folly: that they name the angels, who are free of every deficiency, with the names of females.

This is because they claimed that they are the daughters of Allah, so they made them females and named them daughters.

﴿And they have no knowledge of it.﴾ This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: they name them with this naming while being ignorant of what they say, for they did not know them, nor did they witness them, nor did that reach them by any of the channels through which informants report. Rather, they said that out of ignorance, error and audacity.

It has been recited as "mā lahum bihā" (they have no knowledge of it), meaning of the angels or of the naming. ﴿They follow only conjecture.﴾ That is: in this saying they follow nothing but mere conjecture and imagination. Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about conjecture and its ruling, saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth.﴾ That is: indeed the category of conjecture does not avail anything against the truth in terms of being sufficient, and "the truth" here means knowledge.

In this there is evidence that mere conjecture does not stand in the place of knowledge, and that the one who conjectures is not a person of knowledge.

This applies to matters in which knowledge is required, which are the theoretical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿilmiyyah), not to matters in which conjecture suffices, which are the practical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿamaliyyah). We have already discussed the verification of this.

This specification is necessary, for the indicative force of general expressions (ʿumūm), analogy (qiyās), solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid) and the like is conjectural, so acting upon them is acting upon conjecture. Yet we are obliged to act upon it in matters of this kind. Thus the evidences that make acting upon it obligatory specify this generality, and what has come in its meaning of censure toward one who acts upon conjecture and prohibition from following it.

﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance.﴾ That is: turn away from the one who has turned away from Our remembrance. By "remembrance" here is meant the Qur'an, or the remembrance of the Hereafter, or the remembrance of Allah in general. It has been said that by "remembrance" here is meant faith. The meaning is: leave off disputing with them, for you have conveyed to them what you were commanded, and there is upon you nothing but the conveying. This is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). ﴿And he desires nothing but the worldly life.﴾ That is: he does not desire anything other than it, nor seek anything else, but has limited his view to it. For he is not fit for good, nor deserving of being cared for.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, belittled their state and made their matter insignificant, saying: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge.﴾ That is: that turning away and confining their desire to the worldly life is the extent of their knowledge; they have nothing beyond it, and they do not turn to anything else of the affair of religion.

Al-Farrāʾ said: That is the measure of their intellects and the limit of their knowledge, that they preferred the world over the Hereafter. It has been said that the reference in His words "that" is to their making the angels daughters of Allah and their naming them with the names of females. The first is preferable.

By "knowledge" here is meant general perception, under which false conjecture falls. The sentence is independent, establishing their ignorance and their following of mere conjecture. It has been said that it is an interjected clause between what is being explained and its cause, which is His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided.﴾ For this is the reason for the command to turn away. The meaning is: He, glory be to Him, knows best who has deviated from the truth and turned away from it and was not guided to it, and knows best who was guided, accepted the truth, turned toward it and acted upon it. So He recompenses every doer according to his deed: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and guidance for him not to exhaust himself in calling those who insist upon error and for whom wretchedness has preceded. For Allah has known the state of this straying group just as He has known the state of the rightly guided group.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about the breadth of His power and the greatness of His dominion, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ That is: He is the owner of that and its disposer, none shares with Him in it. The lām in ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾ is connected to what the context indicates, as if He said: He is the owner of that, He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, in order to recompense the evildoer for his evil and the doer of good for his good.

It has been said that His words ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are an interjected clause, and the meaning is: Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and He knows best who is guided, so that He may recompense. It has been said that it is the lām of consequence: that is, the consequence of the affair of creation, among whom are the doer of good and the doer of evil, is that Allah recompenses each of them for his deed.

Makkī said: the lām is connected to His words ﴿Their intercession will avail them nothing﴾, but this is remote both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning.

The majority read ﴿liyajziya﴾ with the third-person (yāʾ). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read it with the first-person plural (nūn). As for ﴿bi-l-ḥusnā﴾, the meaning is: with the good reward, which is Paradise, or because of their good deeds.

Then He described these good doers, saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the grave immoralities.﴾ This relative clause is in the accusative position, as an attribute (naʿt) of the first relative in His words ﴿those who did good﴾. The majority read ﴿kabāʾir﴾ in the plural. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read ﴿kabīr﴾ in the singular. It has been said: the major sins are polytheism and the immoralities are fornication. We have already discussed in the surah of al-Nisāʾ what is more extensive and more beneficial than this.

And the saying of another:

"When you come to us, you will visit us at our dwellings, and you will find firewood, thick and blazing fire."

From this is "ilmām al-khayāl" (the passing of a phantom).

Al-Aʿshā said:

"A phantom from Qutaylah passed by after her cord had been severed from our cord and cut off."

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "alamma al-rajul" means he committed minor sins, and it is said it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Another recited:

"With Zaynab, approach me before the caravan departs, and say: if you have grown weary of us, the heart has not grown weary of you."

The scholars differed in interpreting this lamam mentioned in the verse. The majority hold that it means minor sins. It has been said it is what falls short of fornication, such as a kiss, a glance, or a look. It has been said it is the man who approaches a sin and then repents. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and others said this, and from it is the saying:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much; and what servant of Yours is there who has not approached sin?"

Al-Zajjāj preferred this view, as did al-Naḥḥās. It has been said it is the sins of the Jāhiliyyah, for Allah does not hold one accountable for them in Islam. Niftawayh said: it is that a person commits a sin he was not accustomed to. He said: the Arabs say, "you do not visit us except occasionally," that is, from time to time. He said: it is not that one approaches and does not act, because the Arabs do not say "he approached us" except when he has acted, not when he intended and did not act. The more preferred is the first view.

His words ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ are a justification for what the exception contains: that is, even if that [minor sin] is outside the ruling of being held accountable, it is nonetheless a sin that requires the forgiveness of Allah and needs His mercy. It has been said that He, glory be to Him, forgives whoever repents from his sin.

Then He mentioned His comprehensive knowledge of the states of His servants, saying: ﴿He knows you best when He produced you from the earth.﴾ That is: He created you from it within the creation of your father Ādam. It has been said that the intended is Ādam, for He created him from clay. ﴿And when you were embryos﴾ That is: He knows best your state at the time you were embryos. The word ajinnah is the plural of janīn, which is the child as long as it is in the womb; it was so named because of its being concealed (ijtinān), that is, its being hidden. For this reason He said ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾. So one who has come out of the womb is not called a janīn. The sentence is independent, establishing what precedes it. ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ That is: do not praise yourselves, do not declare yourselves free of sins, and do not commend yourselves. For abandoning the self-justification of the soul is further from ostentation (riyāʾ) and closer to humility (khushūʿ). The sentence ﴿He knows best who has been righteous﴾ is independent, confirming the prohibition: that is, He knows best who has been mindful of Allah's punishment and sincerely directed his deed to Him.

Al-Ḥasan said: Allah, glory be to Him, knows of every soul what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, had explained the ignorance of the polytheists in general, He singled out some of them for censure, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is: who turned away from good and turned aside from following the truth.

﴿And gave little and then held back.﴾ That is: he gave a small gift, or gave something little, then cut that off and withheld from it. The origin of akdā is from kudyah, which is hardness. It is said of one who dug a well and then reached a rock in which digging was impossible for him: "he has akdā." Then the Arabs used it for one who gave but did not complete, and for one who sought something but did not reach its end. From it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"He gave little, then his giving was cut off; and whoever spends kindness among people is praised."

Al-Kisāʾī and Abū Zayd said: it is said "his fingers were hardened" when they were worn out from digging; and "his hand became hard" when it was tired and did not accomplish anything; and "the land became hard" when its vegetation became scant; and "I made the man hold back from the thing" when I turned him away from it; and "the man held back" when his goodness became scant.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of the verse is: he withheld from the gift and cut it off.

Al-Mubarrad said: he refused with a severe refusal.

Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, but some of the polytheists reproached him, so he abandoned it and returned to his polytheism.

Muqātil said: al-Walīd had praised the Qur'an, then withheld from it, so he gave a little of his tongue's goodness and then cut it off.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: it was revealed concerning Abū Jahl.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning is: does this one who withheld have knowledge of what is hidden from him of the matter of punishment, so that he knows it?

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā﴾ ﴿and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ That is: has he not been told and has he not been given news of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā, meaning his books, which are the Torah; and of what is in the scriptures of Ibrāhīm who fulfilled: that is, who completed and perfected what he was commanded.

The exegetes said: that is, he conveyed to his people what he was commanded and delivered it to them. It has been said: he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he had covenanted with Allah.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained what is in their two scriptures, saying: ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.﴾ That is: no soul bearing a burden will carry the burden of another soul. Its meaning is: no soul will be seized for the sin of another. Here "that" (an) is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence following it. The position of the sentence is in the genitive as an appositive (badal) of "the scriptures of Mūsā and the scriptures of Ibrāhīm," or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The tafsīr of this verse has already passed in the surah of al-Anʿām.

**Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani, commentary on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. It is coordinated with His saying ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this too is among what is in the scrolls of Musa (Moses). The meaning is: he has no reward except the recompense of his effort and the requital of his deeds, and no one's deed benefits anyone else. This general statement is specified (*makhsus*) by such verses as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur: 21], and by what is reported concerning the intercession of the prophets and angels for the servants, the legitimacy of the living supplicating for the dead, and similar matters. Whoever said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) by such matters has not been correct, for a specific text does not abrogate a general one; rather, it specifies it. Thus, every proof that establishes that a person benefits from something that is not of his own striving is a specifier for the generality contained in this verse.

﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾: that is, it will be presented to him and disclosed to him on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then he will be recompensed for it﴾: that is, a person will be recompensed for his effort. One says, "Allah recompensed him for his deed" and "recompensed him for his deed" (using different prepositions).

The pronoun in the nominative (the subject of the verb) refers to the man, and the pronoun in the accusative (the object) refers to his effort.

It has been said that the accusative pronoun refers to the recompense mentioned later, which is His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾. In that case the pronoun refers to something mentioned after it, which explains it. It is also permissible for the accusative pronoun to refer to the recompense (*al-jaza'*), which is the verbal noun of *yujziyahu*, and for ﴿the fullest recompense﴾ to be an explanation of the recompense implied by the verb, as in His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. Al-Akhfash said: "One says *jazaytuhu al-jaza'* and *jazaytuhu bil-jaza'*, and there is no difference between them."

﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾: that is, the return and the destination are to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else, so He will requite them for their deeds.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾, that he said: "The major sins are those for which Allah has named the Fire as a punishment, and the immoralities are those for which there is a prescribed legal penalty (*hadd*) in this world."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more resembling *al-lamam* (minor lapses) than what Abu Hurayrah reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eye is the look, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private part confirms this or denies it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The adultery of the two eyes is looking, the adultery of the two lips is kissing, the adultery of the two hands is grasping, and the adultery of the two feet is walking. The private part confirms this or denies it. If he has gone as far as his private part, he is an adulterer; otherwise, it is *al-lamam*."

Musaddad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah that he was asked about His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, and he said: "They are the glance, the squeeze, the kiss and the touching. When the circumcised part touches the circumcised part, the ritual bath becomes obligatory, and that is adultery."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it authentic, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It is the man who commits an immorality and then repents from it."

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
But which of Your servants has not committed lapses?"*

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It means except what has already passed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The *lamma* (lapse) of adultery is when one commits it, then repents and does not return to it; and the *lamma* of drinking wine is when one drinks it, then repents and does not return to it. That is *al-ilmam* (the occasional lapse)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*Al-lamam* is everything between the two limits: the limit of this world and the limit of the Hereafter. It is expiated by the prayer, and it is less than every offence that carries a legal consequence. As for the limit of this world, it is every prescribed penalty that Allah has ordained in this world. As for the limit of the Hereafter, it is everything that Allah has concluded with the Fire, deferring its punishment until the Hereafter."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* reported from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, when a young child of theirs died, would say, 'He is a *siddiq* (a truthful one).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'The Jews have lied. There is no soul that Allah creates in its mother's womb except that it is either wretched or blessed.' Then Allah revealed at that point ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾, the whole verse."

Ahmad, Muslim and Abu Dawud reported "from Zaynab bint Abi Salamah, that she was named Barrah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not praise yourselves; Allah knows best who is truly righteous among you. Name her Zaynab.'" (p-1424)

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and gave little and held back﴾, that he said: "He cut off. It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "He obeyed a little, then stopped."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab* and al-Daylami reported, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Do you know what His saying ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ means?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He fulfilled his day's work with four rak'ahs which he prayed, and he claimed that they were the prayer of *al-Duha* (the forenoon)." In its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is weak.

al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The shares of Islam are thirty shares, which no one completed before Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Allah said: ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾."

Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning the verse, that he said: "It means Ibrahim, who completed obedience in what he did with his son when he saw the vision. And what is in the scrolls of Musa is ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas, from his father, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled? He used to say every morning and evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17], to the end of the verse." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When *al-Najm* was revealed, and it reached ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾, he said: 'He fulfilled ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to His saying ﴿of the warnings of old﴾.'"

Abu Dawud, al-Nahhas (both in *al-Nasikh*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. Then Allah revealed after that ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. So Allah admitted the children into Paradise because of the righteousness of their fathers."

Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾, ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾, ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾, would say *istirja'* (*inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un*) and would humble himself."

al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad* and al-Baghawi in his *Tafsir* reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, that he said: "There is no reflecting on the Lord (*la fikrah fi al-Rabb*)."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 1 of 2):**

His words: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ That is, these people who do not believe in resurrection and what follows it of the Abode of the Hereafter, namely the disbelievers, add to their disbelief an abominable saying and an ignorant folly: that they name the angels, who are free of every deficiency, with the names of females.

This is because they claimed that they are the daughters of Allah, so they made them females and named them daughters.

﴿And they have no knowledge of it.﴾ This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: they name them with this naming while being ignorant of what they say, for they did not know them, nor did they witness them, nor did that reach them by any of the channels through which informants report. Rather, they said that out of ignorance, error and audacity.

It has been recited as "mā lahum bihā" (they have no knowledge of it), meaning of the angels or of the naming. ﴿They follow only conjecture.﴾ That is: in this saying they follow nothing but mere conjecture and imagination. Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about conjecture and its ruling, saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth.﴾ That is: indeed the category of conjecture does not avail anything against the truth in terms of being sufficient, and "the truth" here means knowledge.

In this there is evidence that mere conjecture does not stand in the place of knowledge, and that the one who conjectures is not a person of knowledge.

This applies to matters in which knowledge is required, which are the theoretical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿilmiyyah), not to matters in which conjecture suffices, which are the practical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿamaliyyah). We have already discussed the verification of this.

This specification is necessary, for the indicative force of general expressions (ʿumūm), analogy (qiyās), solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid) and the like is conjectural, so acting upon them is acting upon conjecture. Yet we are obliged to act upon it in matters of this kind. Thus the evidences that make acting upon it obligatory specify this generality, and what has come in its meaning of censure toward one who acts upon conjecture and prohibition from following it.

﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance.﴾ That is: turn away from the one who has turned away from Our remembrance. By "remembrance" here is meant the Qur'an, or the remembrance of the Hereafter, or the remembrance of Allah in general. It has been said that by "remembrance" here is meant faith. The meaning is: leave off disputing with them, for you have conveyed to them what you were commanded, and there is upon you nothing but the conveying. This is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). ﴿And he desires nothing but the worldly life.﴾ That is: he does not desire anything other than it, nor seek anything else, but has limited his view to it. For he is not fit for good, nor deserving of being cared for.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, belittled their state and made their matter insignificant, saying: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge.﴾ That is: that turning away and confining their desire to the worldly life is the extent of their knowledge; they have nothing beyond it, and they do not turn to anything else of the affair of religion.

Al-Farrāʾ said: That is the measure of their intellects and the limit of their knowledge, that they preferred the world over the Hereafter. It has been said that the reference in His words "that" is to their making the angels daughters of Allah and their naming them with the names of females. The first is preferable.

By "knowledge" here is meant general perception, under which false conjecture falls. The sentence is independent, establishing their ignorance and their following of mere conjecture. It has been said that it is an interjected clause between what is being explained and its cause, which is His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided.﴾ For this is the reason for the command to turn away. The meaning is: He, glory be to Him, knows best who has deviated from the truth and turned away from it and was not guided to it, and knows best who was guided, accepted the truth, turned toward it and acted upon it. So He recompenses every doer according to his deed: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and guidance for him not to exhaust himself in calling those who insist upon error and for whom wretchedness has preceded. For Allah has known the state of this straying group just as He has known the state of the rightly guided group.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about the breadth of His power and the greatness of His dominion, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ That is: He is the owner of that and its disposer, none shares with Him in it. The lām in ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾ is connected to what the context indicates, as if He said: He is the owner of that, He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, in order to recompense the evildoer for his evil and the doer of good for his good.

It has been said that His words ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are an interjected clause, and the meaning is: Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and He knows best who is guided, so that He may recompense. It has been said that it is the lām of consequence: that is, the consequence of the affair of creation, among whom are the doer of good and the doer of evil, is that Allah recompenses each of them for his deed.

Makkī said: the lām is connected to His words ﴿Their intercession will avail them nothing﴾, but this is remote both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning.

The majority read ﴿liyajziya﴾ with the third-person (yāʾ). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read it with the first-person plural (nūn). As for ﴿bi-l-ḥusnā﴾, the meaning is: with the good reward, which is Paradise, or because of their good deeds.

Then He described these good doers, saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the grave immoralities.﴾ This relative clause is in the accusative position, as an attribute (naʿt) of the first relative in His words ﴿those who did good﴾. It has been said that it is an appositive (badal) of it, and it has been said that it is an explanatory apposition (bayān) of it, and it has been said that it is in the accusative as an expression of praise (madḥ) with an implied "I mean" (aʿnī), or it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, they avoid the major sins.

The majority read ﴿kabāʾir﴾ in the plural. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read ﴿kabīr﴾ in the singular. The "major sins" (kabāʾir) are every sin for which Allah has threatened the Fire, or whose doer He has censured with severe censure. The scholars have a lengthy discussion on the verification of the major sins.

Just as they differed over the verification of their meaning and reality, they differed over their number. The "immoralities" (fawāḥish) is the plural of fāḥishah, which is what is most heinous among the major sins, such as fornication and the like.

Muqātil said: the major sins of wrongdoing are every sin that is concluded with the Fire, and the immoralities are every sin for which there is a prescribed legal penalty (ḥadd).

It has been said: the major sins are polytheism and the immoralities are fornication. We have already discussed in the surah of al-Nisāʾ what is more extensive and more beneficial than this.

The exception in His words ﴿except the lamam﴾ is disjunct (munqaṭiʿ). The root of lamam in the language is what is little and small. From it: "he visited the place" means he stayed there briefly, and "he took a little of the food" means he ate little of it.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of lamam is that you approach a thing without mounting it: it is said "alamma bi-kadhā" when he approached it and did not mix with it.

Al-Azharī said: the Arabs use "al-ilmām" to mean drawing near and closeness, and from it is the saying of Jarīr:

"By my soul, the one whose avoidance is hard upon me, and whose visit is but a fleeting approach."

And the saying of another:

"When you come to us, you will visit us at our dwellings, and you will find firewood, thick and blazing fire."

Al-Zajjāj said: the origin of lamam and ilmām is what a person does time after time, without going deep into it or persisting in it. It is said: "I approached it" when I visited it and departed from it. And it is said: "I did not do it except occasionally" (lamāman wa ilmāman), that is, from time to time. From this is "ilmām al-khayāl" (the passing of a phantom).

Al-Aʿshā said:

"A phantom from Qutaylah passed by after her cord had been severed from our cord and cut off."

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "alamma al-rajul" means he committed minor sins, and it is said it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Another recited:

"With Zaynab, approach me before the caravan departs, and say: if you have grown weary of us, the heart has not grown weary of you."

The scholars differed in interpreting this lamam mentioned in the verse. The majority hold that it means minor sins. It has been said it is what falls short of fornication, such as a kiss, a glance, or a look. It has been said it is the man who approaches a sin and then repents. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and others said this, and from it is the saying:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much; and what servant of Yours is there who has not approached sin?"

Al-Zajjāj preferred this view, as did al-Naḥḥās. It has been said it is the sins of the Jāhiliyyah, for Allah does not hold one accountable for them in Islam. Niftawayh said: it is that a person commits a sin he was not accustomed to. He said: the Arabs say, "you do not visit us except occasionally," that is, from time to time. He said: it is not that one approaches and does not act, because the Arabs do not say "he approached us" except when he has acted, not when he intended and did not act. The more preferred is the first view.

His words ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ are a justification for what the exception contains: that is, even if that [minor sin] is outside the ruling of being held accountable, it is nonetheless a sin that requires the forgiveness of Allah and needs His mercy. It has been said that He, glory be to Him, forgives whoever repents from his sin.

Then He mentioned His comprehensive knowledge of the states of His servants, saying: ﴿He knows you best when He produced you from the earth.﴾ That is: He created you from it within the creation of your father Ādam. It has been said that the intended is Ādam, for He created him from clay. ﴿And when you were embryos﴾ That is: He knows best your state at the time you were embryos. The word ajinnah is the plural of janīn, which is the child as long as it is in the womb; it was so named because of its being concealed (ijtinān), that is, its being hidden. For this reason He said ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾. So one who has come out of the womb is not called a janīn. The sentence is independent, establishing what precedes it. ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ That is: do not praise yourselves, do not declare yourselves free of sins, and do not commend yourselves. For abandoning the self-justification of the soul is further from ostentation (riyāʾ) and closer to humility (khushūʿ). The sentence ﴿He knows best who has been righteous﴾ is independent, confirming the prohibition: that is, He knows best who has been mindful of Allah's punishment and sincerely directed his deed to Him.

Al-Ḥasan said: Allah, glory be to Him, knows of every soul what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, had explained the ignorance of the polytheists in general, He singled out some of them for censure, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is: who turned away from good and turned aside from following the truth.

﴿And gave little and then held back.﴾ That is: he gave a small gift, or gave something little, then cut that off and withheld from it. The origin of akdā is from kudyah, which is hardness. It is said of one who dug a well and then reached a rock in which digging was impossible for him: "he has akdā." Then the Arabs used it for one who gave but did not complete, and for one who sought something but did not reach its end. From it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"He gave little, then his giving was cut off; and whoever spends kindness among people is praised."

Al-Kisāʾī and Abū Zayd said: it is said "his fingers were hardened" when they were worn out from digging; and "his hand became hard" when it was tired and did not accomplish anything; and "the land became hard" when its vegetation became scant; and "I made the man hold back from the thing" when I turned him away from it; and "the man held back" when his goodness became scant.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of the verse is: he withheld from the gift and cut it off.

Al-Mubarrad said: he refused with a severe refusal.

Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, but some of the polytheists reproached him, so he abandoned it and returned to his polytheism.

Muqātil said: al-Walīd had praised the Qur'an, then withheld from it, so he gave a little of his tongue's goodness and then cut it off.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: it was revealed concerning Abū Jahl.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning is: does this one who withheld have knowledge of what is hidden from him of the matter of punishment, so that he knows it?

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā﴾ ﴿and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ That is: has he not been told and has he not been given news of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā, meaning his books, which are the Torah; and of what is in the scriptures of Ibrāhīm who fulfilled: that is, who completed and perfected what he was commanded.

The exegetes said: that is, he conveyed to his people what he was commanded and delivered it to them. It has been said: he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he had covenanted with Allah.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained what is in their two scriptures, saying: ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.﴾ That is: no soul bearing a burden will carry the burden of another soul. Its meaning is: no soul will be seized for the sin of another. Here "that" (an) is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence following it. The position of the sentence is in the genitive as an appositive (badal) of "the scriptures of Mūsā and the scriptures of Ibrāhīm," or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The tafsīr of this verse has already passed in the surah of al-Anʿām.

**Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani, commentary on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. It is coordinated with His saying ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this too is among what is in the scrolls of Musa (Moses). The meaning is: he has no reward except the recompense of his effort and the requital of his deeds, and no one's deed benefits anyone else. This general statement is specified (*makhsus*) by such verses as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur: 21], and by what is reported concerning the intercession of the prophets and angels for the servants, the legitimacy of the living supplicating for the dead, and similar matters. Whoever said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) by such matters has not been correct, for a specific text does not abrogate a general one; rather, it specifies it. Thus, every proof that establishes that a person benefits from something that is not of his own striving is a specifier for the generality contained in this verse.

﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾: that is, it will be presented to him and disclosed to him on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then he will be recompensed for it﴾: that is, a person will be recompensed for his effort. One says, "Allah recompensed him for his deed" and "recompensed him for his deed" (using different prepositions).

The pronoun in the nominative (the subject of the verb) refers to the man, and the pronoun in the accusative (the object) refers to his effort.

It has been said that the accusative pronoun refers to the recompense mentioned later, which is His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾. In that case the pronoun refers to something mentioned after it, which explains it. It is also permissible for the accusative pronoun to refer to the recompense (*al-jaza'*), which is the verbal noun of *yujziyahu*, and for ﴿the fullest recompense﴾ to be an explanation of the recompense implied by the verb, as in His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. Al-Akhfash said: "One says *jazaytuhu al-jaza'* and *jazaytuhu bil-jaza'*, and there is no difference between them."

﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾: that is, the return and the destination are to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else, so He will requite them for their deeds.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾, that he said: "The major sins are those for which Allah has named the Fire as a punishment, and the immoralities are those for which there is a prescribed legal penalty (*hadd*) in this world."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more resembling *al-lamam* (minor lapses) than what Abu Hurayrah reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eye is the look, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private part confirms this or denies it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The adultery of the two eyes is looking, the adultery of the two lips is kissing, the adultery of the two hands is grasping, and the adultery of the two feet is walking. The private part confirms this or denies it. If he has gone as far as his private part, he is an adulterer; otherwise, it is *al-lamam*."

Musaddad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah that he was asked about His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, and he said: "They are the glance, the squeeze, the kiss and the touching. When the circumcised part touches the circumcised part, the ritual bath becomes obligatory, and that is adultery."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it authentic, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It is the man who commits an immorality and then repents from it."

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
But which of Your servants has not committed lapses?"*

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "It means except what has already passed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying ﴿except minor lapses﴾, that he said: "The *lamma* (lapse) of adultery is when one commits it, then repents and does not return to it; and the *lamma* of drinking wine is when one drinks it, then repents and does not return to it. That is *al-ilmam* (the occasional lapse)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*Al-lamam* is everything between the two limits: the limit of this world and the limit of the Hereafter. It is expiated by the prayer, and it is less than every offence that carries a legal consequence. As for the limit of this world, it is every prescribed penalty that Allah has ordained in this world. As for the limit of the Hereafter, it is everything that Allah has concluded with the Fire, deferring its punishment until the Hereafter."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* reported from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, when a young child of theirs died, would say, 'He is a *siddiq* (a truthful one).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'The Jews have lied. There is no soul that Allah creates in its mother's womb except that it is either wretched or blessed.' Then Allah revealed at that point ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾, the whole verse."

Ahmad, Muslim and Abu Dawud reported "from Zaynab bint Abi Salamah, that she was named Barrah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not praise yourselves; Allah knows best who is truly righteous among you. Name her Zaynab.'" (p-1424)

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and gave little and held back﴾, that he said: "He cut off. It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "He obeyed a little, then stopped."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab* and al-Daylami reported, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Do you know what His saying ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ means?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He fulfilled his day's work with four rak'ahs which he prayed, and he claimed that they were the prayer of *al-Duha* (the forenoon)." In its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is weak.

al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The shares of Islam are thirty shares, which no one completed before Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Allah said: ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾."

Ibn Jarir reported from him concerning the verse, that he said: "It means Ibrahim, who completed obedience in what he did with his son when he saw the vision. And what is in the scrolls of Musa is ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas, from his father, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled? He used to say every morning and evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17], to the end of the verse." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When *al-Najm* was revealed, and it reached ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾, he said: 'He fulfilled ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, to His saying ﴿of the warnings of old﴾.'"

Abu Dawud, al-Nahhas (both in *al-Nasikh*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. Then Allah revealed after that ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. So Allah admitted the children into Paradise because of the righteousness of their fathers."

Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾, ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾, ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾, would say *istirja'* (*inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un*) and would humble himself."

al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad* and al-Baghawi in his *Tafsir* reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, that he said: "There is no reflecting on the Lord (*la fikrah fi al-Rabb*)."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 1 of 2):**

His words: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ That is, these people who do not believe in resurrection and what follows it of the Abode of the Hereafter, namely the disbelievers, add to their disbelief an abominable saying and an ignorant folly: that they name the angels, who are free of every deficiency, with the names of females.

This is because they claimed that they are the daughters of Allah, so they made them females and named them daughters.

﴿And they have no knowledge of it.﴾ This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: they name them with this naming while being ignorant of what they say, for they did not know them, nor did they witness them, nor did that reach them by any of the channels through which informants report. Rather, they said that out of ignorance, error and audacity.

It has been recited as "mā lahum bihā" (they have no knowledge of it), meaning of the angels or of the naming. ﴿They follow only conjecture.﴾ That is: in this saying they follow nothing but mere conjecture and imagination. Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about conjecture and its ruling, saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth.﴾ That is: indeed the category of conjecture does not avail anything against the truth in terms of being sufficient, and "the truth" here means knowledge.

In this there is evidence that mere conjecture does not stand in the place of knowledge, and that the one who conjectures is not a person of knowledge.

This applies to matters in which knowledge is required, which are the theoretical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿilmiyyah), not to matters in which conjecture suffices, which are the practical questions (al-masāʾil al-ʿamaliyyah). We have already discussed the verification of this.

This specification is necessary, for the indicative force of general expressions (ʿumūm), analogy (qiyās), solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid) and the like is conjectural, so acting upon them is acting upon conjecture. Yet we are obliged to act upon it in matters of this kind. Thus the evidences that make acting upon it obligatory specify this generality, and what has come in its meaning of censure toward one who acts upon conjecture and prohibition from following it.

﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance.﴾ That is: turn away from the one who has turned away from Our remembrance. By "remembrance" here is meant the Qur'an, or the remembrance of the Hereafter, or the remembrance of Allah in general. It has been said that by "remembrance" here is meant faith. The meaning is: leave off disputing with them, for you have conveyed to them what you were commanded, and there is upon you nothing but the conveying. This is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). ﴿And he desires nothing but the worldly life.﴾ That is: he does not desire anything other than it, nor seek anything else, but has limited his view to it. For he is not fit for good, nor deserving of being cared for.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, belittled their state and made their matter insignificant, saying: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge.﴾ That is: that turning away and confining their desire to the worldly life is the extent of their knowledge; they have nothing beyond it, and they do not turn to anything else of the affair of religion.

Al-Farrāʾ said: That is the measure of their intellects and the limit of their knowledge, that they preferred the world over the Hereafter. It has been said that the reference in His words "that" is to their making the angels daughters of Allah and their naming them with the names of females. The first is preferable.

By "knowledge" here is meant general perception, under which false conjecture falls. The sentence is independent, establishing their ignorance and their following of mere conjecture. It has been said that it is an interjected clause between what is being explained and its cause, which is His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided.﴾ For this is the reason for the command to turn away. The meaning is: He, glory be to Him, knows best who has deviated from the truth and turned away from it and was not guided to it, and knows best who was guided, accepted the truth, turned toward it and acted upon it. So He recompenses every doer according to his deed: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and guidance for him not to exhaust himself in calling those who insist upon error and for whom wretchedness has preceded. For Allah has known the state of this straying group just as He has known the state of the rightly guided group.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed about the breadth of His power and the greatness of His dominion, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ That is: He is the owner of that and its disposer, none shares with Him in it. The lām in ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾ is connected to what the context indicates, as if He said: He is the owner of that, He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, in order to recompense the evildoer for his evil and the doer of good for his good.

It has been said that His words ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are an interjected clause, and the meaning is: Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and He knows best who is guided, so that He may recompense. It has been said that it is the lām of consequence: that is, the consequence of the affair of creation, among whom are the doer of good and the doer of evil, is that Allah recompenses each of them for his deed.

Makkī said: the lām is connected to His words ﴿Their intercession will avail them nothing﴾, but this is remote both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning.

The majority read ﴿liyajziya﴾ with the third-person (yāʾ). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read it with the first-person plural (nūn). As for ﴿bi-l-ḥusnā﴾, the meaning is: with the good reward, which is Paradise, or because of their good deeds.

Then He described these good doers, saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the grave immoralities.﴾ This relative clause is in the accusative position, as an attribute (naʿt) of the first relative in His words ﴿those who did good﴾. It has been said that it is an appositive (badal) of it, and it has been said that it is an explanatory apposition (bayān) of it, and it has been said that it is in the accusative as an expression of praise (madḥ) with an implied "I mean" (aʿnī), or it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, they avoid the major sins.

The majority read ﴿kabāʾir﴾ in the plural. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read ﴿kabīr﴾ in the singular. The "major sins" (kabāʾir) are every sin for which Allah has threatened the Fire, or whose doer He has censured with severe censure. The scholars have a lengthy discussion on the verification of the major sins.

Just as they differed over the verification of their meaning and reality, they differed over their number. The "immoralities" (fawāḥish) is the plural of fāḥishah, which is what is most heinous among the major sins, such as fornication and the like.

Muqātil said: the major sins of wrongdoing are every sin that is concluded with the Fire, and the immoralities are every sin for which there is a prescribed legal penalty (ḥadd).

It has been said: the major sins are polytheism and the immoralities are fornication. We have already discussed in the surah of al-Nisāʾ what is more extensive and more beneficial than this.

The exception in His words ﴿except the lamam﴾ is disjunct (munqaṭiʿ). The root of lamam in the language is what is little and small. From it: "he visited the place" means he stayed there briefly, and "he took a little of the food" means he ate little of it.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of lamam is that you approach a thing without mounting it: it is said "alamma bi-kadhā" when he approached it and did not mix with it.

Al-Azharī said: the Arabs use "al-ilmām" to mean drawing near and closeness, and from it is the saying of Jarīr:

"By my soul, the one whose avoidance is hard upon me, and whose visit is but a fleeting approach."

And the saying of another:

"When you come to us, you will visit us at our dwellings, and you will find firewood, thick and blazing fire."

Al-Zajjāj said: the origin of lamam and ilmām is what a person does time after time, without going deep into it or persisting in it. It is said: "I approached it" when I visited it and departed from it. And it is said: "I did not do it except occasionally" (lamāman wa ilmāman), that is, from time to time. From this is "ilmām al-khayāl" (the passing of a phantom).

Al-Aʿshā said:

"A phantom from Qutaylah passed by after her cord had been severed from our cord and cut off."

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "alamma al-rajul" means he committed minor sins, and it is said it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Another recited:

"With Zaynab, approach me before the caravan departs, and say: if you have grown weary of us, the heart has not grown weary of you."

The scholars differed in interpreting this lamam mentioned in the verse. The majority hold that it means minor sins. It has been said it is what falls short of fornication, such as a kiss, a glance, or a look. It has been said it is the man who approaches a sin and then repents. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and others said this, and from it is the saying:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much; and what servant of Yours is there who has not approached sin?"

Al-Zajjāj preferred this view, as did al-Naḥḥās. It has been said it is the sins of the Jāhiliyyah, for Allah does not hold one accountable for them in Islam. Niftawayh said: it is that a person commits a sin he was not accustomed to. He said: the Arabs say, "you do not visit us except occasionally," that is, from time to time. He said: it is not that one approaches and does not act, because the Arabs do not say "he approached us" except when he has acted, not when he intended and did not act. The more preferred is the first view.

His words ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ are a justification for what the exception contains: that is, even if that [minor sin] is outside the ruling of being held accountable, it is nonetheless a sin that requires the forgiveness of Allah and needs His mercy. It has been said that He, glory be to Him, forgives whoever repents from his sin.

Then He mentioned His comprehensive knowledge of the states of His servants, saying: ﴿He knows you best when He produced you from the earth.﴾ That is: He created you from it within the creation of your father Ādam. It has been said that the intended is Ādam, for He created him from clay. ﴿And when you were embryos﴾ That is: He knows best your state at the time you were embryos. The word ajinnah is the plural of janīn, which is the child as long as it is in the womb; it was so named because of its being concealed (ijtinān), that is, its being hidden. For this reason He said ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾. So one who has come out of the womb is not called a janīn. The sentence is independent, establishing what precedes it. ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾ That is: do not praise yourselves, do not declare yourselves free of sins, and do not commend yourselves. For abandoning the self-justification of the soul is further from ostentation (riyāʾ) and closer to humility (khushūʿ). The sentence ﴿He knows best who has been righteous﴾ is independent, confirming the prohibition: that is, He knows best who has been mindful of Allah's punishment and sincerely directed his deed to Him.

Al-Ḥasan said: Allah, glory be to Him, knows of every soul what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, had explained the ignorance of the polytheists in general, He singled out some of them for censure, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is: who turned away from good and turned aside from following the truth.

﴿And gave little and then held back.﴾ That is: he gave a small gift, or gave something little, then cut that off and withheld from it. The origin of akdā is from kudyah, which is hardness. It is said of one who dug a well and then reached a rock in which digging was impossible for him: "he has akdā." Then the Arabs used it for one who gave but did not complete, and for one who sought something but did not reach its end. From it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"He gave little, then his giving was cut off; and whoever spends kindness among people is praised."

Al-Kisāʾī and Abū Zayd said: it is said "his fingers were hardened" when they were worn out from digging; and "his hand became hard" when it was tired and did not accomplish anything; and "the land became hard" when its vegetation became scant; and "I made the man hold back from the thing" when I turned him away from it; and "the man held back" when his goodness became scant.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of the verse is: he withheld from the gift and cut it off.

Al-Mubarrad said: he refused with a severe refusal.

Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, but some of the polytheists reproached him, so he abandoned it and returned to his polytheism.

Muqātil said: al-Walīd had praised the Qur'an, then withheld from it, so he gave a little of his tongue's goodness and then cut it off.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: it was revealed concerning Abū Jahl.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning is: does this one who withheld have knowledge of what is hidden from him of the matter of punishment, so that he knows it?

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā﴾ ﴿and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ That is: has he not been told and has he not been given news of what is in the scriptures of Mūsā, meaning his books, which are the Torah; and of what is in the scriptures of Ibrāhīm who fulfilled: that is, who completed and perfected what he was commanded.

The exegetes said: that is, he conveyed to his people what he was commanded and delivered it to them. It has been said: he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he had covenanted with Allah.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained what is in their two scriptures, saying: ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.﴾ That is: no soul bearing a burden will carry the burden of another soul. Its meaning is: no soul will be seized for the sin of another. Here "that" (an) is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence following it. The position of the sentence is in the genitive as an appositive (badal) of "the scriptures of Mūsā and the scriptures of Ibrāhīm," or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The tafsīr of this verse has already passed in the surah of al-Anʿām.

**Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani, commentary on surah 53, verses 27–42 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. It is coordinated with His saying ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this too is among what is in the scrolls of Musa (Moses). The meaning is: he has no reward except the recompense of his effort and the requital of his deeds, and no one's deed benefits anyone else. This general statement is specified (*makhsus*) by such verses as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur: 21], and by what is reported concerning the intercession of the prophets and angels for the servants, the legitimacy of the living supplicating for the dead, and similar matters. Whoever said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) by such matters has not been correct, for a specific text does not abrogate a general one; rather, it specifies it. Thus, every proof that establishes that a person benefits from something that is not of his own striving is a specifier for the generality contained in this verse.
